trades-creative-service-2.title: Hunar: Shop, freelance & farm
trades-creative-service-2.description: Run a shop with healthy margins, earn online as a freelancer without falling for scams, and grow food — from a balcony garden to farming as a business.

courses.title: Retail and shopkeeping
courses.summary: Lay out a shop that sells, manage stock and margins with real numbers, serve customers and take digital payments safely, and keep simple daily accounts including credit.
outcomes: Learners can plan a shop layout and display using proven retail principles
Learners can calculate markup and margin and set reorder levels
Learners can handle UPI payments safely and know basic consumer rules (MRP, bills)
Learners can keep a daily cash book and manage customer credit (udhaar)

scenes.text: Ramu's kirana store in Mysuru was crowded and dark; customers asked for items and waited while he searched.
His daughter Kavya, a commerce student, suggested better lighting, grouped categories, and price labels.
They placed small impulse items (chocolates, batteries) near the billing counter and essentials where customers walk past other goods.
Within two months, average bill size rose and customers found things themselves.

steps.title: Layout principles
steps.body:
- **Group by category** (staples, snacks, personal care, cleaning) so customers can find things.
- **Essentials deeper inside** — customers walking to buy rice or milk pass other products.
- **Impulse items near billing** — chocolates, gum, small batteries, phone accessories.
- **Clear aisles** and good lighting; nothing blocking the entrance.
- **Price labels** on shelves or products — customers trust visible prices.

steps.title: Display and merchandising
steps.body:
- **Eye level is buy level**: put high-margin or featured items at eye level; kids' items lower.
- **Face products forward** and keep shelves full — empty shelves look like a closing shop.
- **Seasonal displays**: festival items, school supplies in June, umbrellas before monsoon.
- **Clean and dust daily** — a dusty product looks old.

steps.title: FIFO and FEFO
steps.body: Rotate stock so older items sell first: **FIFO** (first in, first out) and, for perishables and medicines, **FEFO** (first expiry, first out). Put new stock at the back, older at the front. Check expiry dates weekly; remove expired goods — selling them harms customers and your reputation and can break the law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Overcrowded shelves, no prices, expired goods mixed with fresh, fast-moving items hidden, and a cluttered counter that slows billing.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Visit a local shop and sketch its layout. Mark where essentials, impulse items and billing are. Suggest three improvements.

activity.prompt: Where would you place each item?

quiz.q: Why put essentials deeper in the shop?
options: So customers pass other products on the way
quiz.why: Putting essentials deeper in the shop means customers walk past other products on the way. More exposure leads to more sales.
FEFO is First Expiry, First Out: sell the items that expire soonest first. It reduces waste from expired goods.

options: Customers buy what they see easily
quiz.why: 'Eye level is buy level' means products placed where people see them easily sell more. Visibility drives sales.
Expired goods must be removed from sale. Selling them harms customers and can get you into legal trouble.

scenes.text: Neha opened a stationery shop near a school in Bhopal. She bought pens at ₹8 and sold at ₹10, thinking she made 25%.
Her accountant uncle explained: 25% is markup on cost; her margin on sales is 20%.
He also showed her a reorder level, so she'd never run out of notebooks in June again.
Neha now plans prices using margin and never misses the school-reopening rush.

steps.title: Markup vs margin
steps.body:
- **Markup** = profit ÷ **cost** × 100.
- **Margin** = profit ÷ **selling price** × 100.

Example: cost ₹80, selling price ₹100, profit ₹20.

- Markup = 20 ÷ 80 = **25%**
- Margin = 20 ÷ 100 = **20%**

Confusing the two makes shopkeepers think they earn more than they do.

steps.title: Setting a price for a target margin
steps.body:
Selling price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin).

Cost ₹60, target margin 25%: 60 ÷ 0.75 = **₹80**. Check: profit ₹20 ÷ ₹80 = 25% ✔.

On packaged goods, you **cannot charge more than the printed MRP** — so your margin is set by your purchase price and the MRP.

steps.title: Reorder level and safety stock
steps.body:
**Reorder level = average daily sales × supplier lead time (days) + safety stock.**

Example: you sell 12 packets of biscuits a day, the distributor takes 3 days, and you keep 10 extra as safety: 12 × 3 + 10 = **46**. When stock falls to 46 packets, reorder.

Too much stock ties up cash and risks expiry; too little loses sales.

steps.title: Know your fast and slow movers
steps.body: Track weekly sales of your top items. Fast movers need reliable reordering; slow movers need less space, smaller orders or offers. A simple notebook or a free billing app can show this.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick three products from a shop. Estimate cost and MRP (ask the shopkeeper if they're willing). Calculate markup and margin for each.

activity.prompt: Cost price ₹150, selling price ₹200. What is the margin on selling price (%)?

quiz.why: Margin is profit on the selling price: (100 − 80) ÷ 100 = 20%. Markup is based on cost, so it's a different number (25%).

quiz.q: Daily sales 10, lead time 4 days, safety stock 8. Reorder level?
quiz.why: Reorder level = daily sales × lead time + safety stock = 10 × 4 + 8 = 48.

quiz.q: Can a shop charge above MRP on packaged goods?
quiz.why: Selling above the printed MRP on packaged goods is not allowed. MRP is the maximum retail price.

scenes.text: A young man at Farida's mobile accessories shop in Pune showed a 'payment successful' screen for ₹1,200 and walked off quickly.
Farida's soundbox hadn't announced anything. She checked her UPI app — no payment.
She learned: always confirm on your own soundbox or app, never the customer's screen.
She now politely waits for her own confirmation for every payment.

steps.title: Taking UPI payments safely
steps.body:
- Display your **own QR code**; check it hasn't been covered or replaced by someone else's.
- **Confirm on your own device** (soundbox, app notification or bank statement) — never trust the customer's screen or a screenshot.
- To **receive** money you never need to enter your UPI PIN. Anyone asking you to 'enter PIN to receive' or 'scan to receive' is scamming you.
- Never share OTPs or PINs with anyone, including callers claiming to be from the bank.
- Report cyber fraud quickly on **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: Customer service that brings people back
steps.body:
- Greet customers; remember regulars' names and preferences.
- If an item is out of stock, offer an alternative or to order it.
- Handle complaints calmly: listen, apologise for the trouble, fix it (exchange/refund as per your policy), thank them.
- Offer home delivery or WhatsApp orders if practical.

steps.title: Consumer rules every shopkeeper should know
steps.body:
- Don't sell packaged goods **above MRP**; weights and measures must be accurate and scales verified as per Legal Metrology rules.
- Give a **bill/receipt** when asked; it builds trust.
- Don't sell expired or unsafe goods.
- Customers can raise complaints under the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, including through the **National Consumer Helpline (1915)**.
- **GST**: registration becomes mandatory above a turnover threshold — generally ₹40 lakh for goods suppliers (lower in some states) and ₹20 lakh for services (lower in some states). Check the GST portal or a tax professional for current rules.

This is general education, not legal or tax advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a polite script for a customer complaint about a damaged product: greet, listen, apologise, offer solution, thank.

a.text: A customer shows you a 'Payment successful ₹850' screen and starts leaving. Your soundbox is silent.

choices.label: Trust the screen and let them go
choices.feedback: Screens and screenshots can be faked.

choices.label: Politely ask them to wait while you check your own app

b.text: No payment in your app. The customer says, 'It's a bank delay, I'll send again — just scan my QR to receive the refund first.'

choices.label: Scan their QR and enter your PIN
choices.feedback: Entering your PIN sends money — you'd lose more.

choices.label: Say you'll wait for the payment to arrive in your app before handing over goods

e1.text: No money arrives. You've lost ₹850 of goods. Always confirm on your own soundbox or app.

e2.text: Money leaves your account. Call 1930 immediately and report on cybercrime.gov.in. Remember: you never need a PIN to receive money.

e3.text: The 'customer' leaves without the goods. You've avoided a common scam.

quiz.q: Do you need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money?
quiz.why: You never need your UPI PIN to receive money. The PIN is only for sending, so a request for it is a scam.

quiz.q: How should you confirm a UPI payment?
quiz.why: Confirm a UPI payment on your own soundbox or app. A customer's word or screen or a screenshot can be faked.

quiz.q: National helpline for cyber financial fraud?
quiz.why: 1930 is India's national helpline for cyber financial fraud.

quiz.q: The National Consumer Helpline number is…
quiz.why: 1915 is the National Consumer Helpline. 1930 is for cyber fraud, and 14416 for mental health.

scenes.text: Gopal's grocery in Varanasi gave credit to many families. His notebook was messy; he forgot who owed what.
At year end, nearly ₹40,000 was stuck, and he had trouble paying his own suppliers.
His son set up a simple credit ledger app, a limit per customer, and polite monthly reminders.
Collections improved and Gopal could restock on time.

steps.title: The daily cash book
steps.body:
Every day, record:

- **Opening cash** (what's in the drawer at start)
- **Sales**: cash and UPI/card separately
- **Expenses**: purchases, electricity, wages, transport
- **Closing cash** (count it)

Opening + cash sales − cash expenses should equal closing cash. A mismatch means an error, a missed entry, or a loss — investigate the same day.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Opening cash ₹2,000. Cash sales ₹6,500. UPI sales ₹4,200 (goes to bank). Cash paid to supplier ₹3,000; tea and transport ₹200.

Expected closing cash = 2,000 + 6,500 − 3,000 − 200 = **₹5,300**.

Total sales for the day = 6,500 + 4,200 = **₹10,700**.

steps.title: Managing credit (udhaar) wisely
steps.body:
- Give credit only to known, regular customers.
- Set a **limit** per customer and a **due date** (e.g. monthly).
- Record every credit sale with date, items, amount — and get the customer to see or confirm it.
- Send polite reminders; many ledger apps send them automatically.
- Stop extra credit until old dues are cleared.
- Keep total credit within what your cash flow can handle.

steps.title: Know your monthly profit
steps.body: Monthly profit = total sales − cost of goods sold − expenses (rent, electricity, wages, transport, etc.). Separate your **personal spending** from the shop's money — mixing them is one of the most common reasons small shops struggle.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For one week, keep a cash book for your own pocket money or household purchases: opening, in, out, closing. Did it balance every day?

activity.prompt: Opening cash ₹1,500. Cash sales ₹5,000. Cash expenses ₹2,300. UPI sales ₹3,000 (to bank). What should closing cash in the drawer be?

quiz.why: Expected closing cash = opening cash + cash sales − cash expenses. It tracks the cash going in and out of the drawer.

options: Limits, due dates and records for regular customers
quiz.why: Good credit practice is to give credit with limits, due dates and written records, to regular customers. Unlimited credit or no records risks losses.

quiz.q: Why separate personal and shop money?
options: To know true profit and keep cash for stock
quiz.why: Separating personal and shop money shows your true profit and keeps cash for stock. Mixing them hides losses.

quiz.q: A cash mismatch at day end should be…
quiz.why: A cash mismatch is easiest to find on the same day, while you remember what happened. Waiting makes it hard to trace.

questions.why: Impulse items are best near the billing counter, where customers wait and make last-minute purchases.
FIFO means First In, First Out: sell the older stock first so it doesn't go bad.

questions.q: To receive UPI money you need to…
options: Do nothing except share your QR/UPI ID
questions.why: To receive UPI money you only need to share your QR code or UPI ID. You never enter a PIN or share an OTP.

questions.q: Cyber fraud helpline in India is…
questions.why: 1930 is India's cyber fraud helpline. 1098 is Childline and 1915 is the consumer helpline.

questions.q: Daily sales 20, lead time 2 days, safety stock 15. Reorder level?
questions.why: Reorder level = daily sales × lead time + safety stock = 20 × 2 + 15 = 55.
A 25% margin means the cost is 75% of the price. So price = 90 ÷ 0.75 = ₹120. Adding 25% to the cost would give ₹112.50, which is a markup.

questions.q: Opening ₹1,000 + cash sales ₹4,000 − cash expenses ₹1,800 = closing?
Why is too much stock a problem?
options: It ties up cash and risks expiry
questions.why: Too much stock ties up cash and risks items expiring or going out of date. Cash is better used in goods that sell.

questions.q: A customer complains about a damaged item. Best first step?
options: Listen calmly and apologise for the trouble
questions.why: With a complaint, first listen calmly and apologise for the trouble. This calms the customer, and then you can solve the problem.

questions.q: A shop owner thinks a 30% markup means 30% of sales is profit. The true margin is about…
questions.why: A 30% markup on cost 100 gives a price of 130 and profit of 30. The margin is 30 ÷ 130 ≈ 23%, not 30%.

courses.title: Digital freelancing: earn online safely
courses.summary: Pick a sellable skill, build a portfolio and profile, price and pitch your work, and protect yourself with contracts, safe payments, tax awareness and scam spotting.
outcomes: Learners can identify a marketable digital skill and a niche
Learners can build a portfolio and a strong profile
Learners can calculate a sustainable rate and write a winning proposal
Learners can use simple contracts, avoid scams and understand tax basics

scenes.text: Aditi, a BCom student in Jaipur, made beautiful notes and slides for friends.
A senior suggested she offer presentation design to small businesses.
She chose a niche — pitch decks for startups and coaching institutes — and practised with three free samples.
Her first paid client came from a LinkedIn post. Six months later, she had steady weekend income.

steps.title: Skills people pay for online
steps.body:
- **Writing**: blogs, website copy, product descriptions, technical writing.
- **Design**: logos, social media posts, presentations, UI/UX.
- **Video and audio**: editing, subtitles, podcasts.
- **Development**: websites, apps, automation, data analysis.
- **Marketing**: social media management, SEO, ads.
- **Language**: translation, transcription, tutoring.
- **Support**: virtual assistance, bookkeeping, customer support.

steps.title: Choose a niche
steps.body: 'I do design' competes with millions. 'I design menus and Instagram posts for cafés' stands out. A niche = **skill × type of client × problem solved**. Start where you already have some skill or knowledge, and where clients can afford to pay.

steps.title: Getting good enough to be paid
steps.body:
- Practise on **real-looking projects**: redesign a local shop's menu, write blogs for an imaginary brand.
- Use free learning resources and practise daily.
- Ask for honest feedback from people in the field.
- Your first goal is not perfection — it's **reliable, on-time, clean** work.

steps.title: Watch out
steps.body: 'Data entry from home — earn ₹30,000 a week, pay ₹999 registration' is almost always a **scam**. Real clients pay you; you don't pay to get work.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your niche sentence: 'I help ___ (client type) with ___ (problem) by ___ (your skill).' Share it with a friend and ask if it's clear.

activity.prompt: List three skills you already have (even partly) and the kind of client who might pay for each. Which one excites you most, and why?
activity.hint: Think of what friends ask you for help with — slides, editing, explaining maths, fixing phones, writing captions.

quiz.why: A strong niche combines your skill, a type of client and a problem you solve. A specific position helps you stand out.

quiz.q: 'Pay ₹999 to register for data-entry work' is likely…
quiz.why: Real clients pay you, not the other way round. Being asked to pay to get data-entry work is a scam.

quiz.q: Your early work should be above all…
quiz.why: Early on, be reliable, on time and clean in your work. Reliability builds reputation and brings repeat clients.

options: Realistic samples like redesigning a local menu
quiz.why: Good practice projects are realistic samples, such as redesigning a local menu. They show your ability, and copying others' work is dishonest.

scenes.text: Rahul, a self-taught video editor in Guwahati, had no reviews on any platform.
He made three short before/after edits and wrote what problem each solved.
His profile headline changed from 'Video editor' to 'Short-form video editor for educators — captions, hooks, retention'.
A teacher with a YouTube channel hired him within two weeks.

steps.title: What a portfolio needs
steps.body:
- **3–6 best pieces**, not everything you've ever made.
- For each: the **problem**, what you did, and the **result** (e.g. 'reduced video length 40%, added captions').
- Before/after where possible.
- Only show work you're allowed to show; never use others' work as your own.
- Host it simply: a free website builder, Behance/Dribbble (design), GitHub (code), or a shared drive folder with a clean index.

steps.title: A profile that converts
steps.body:
- **Headline**: niche + benefit ('Website copy for Indian D2C brands that turns visitors into buyers').
- **Photo**: clear, friendly, professional.
- **About**: who you help, how, proof, and how to contact you.
- **Clear services** with starting prices or packages.
- Keep the same name and style across LinkedIn, platforms and your portfolio.

steps.title: Getting the first reviews
steps.body:
- Do a small paid job at a fair introductory price for a real client.
- Over-communicate, deliver early, and ask politely for a review.
- Turn every finished job into a portfolio piece (with permission).

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Fake reviews, copied portfolios, or claiming skills you don't have. Platforms ban accounts for this, and clients talk.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rewrite your profile headline three ways using 'niche + benefit'. Pick the one a busy client would understand in 3 seconds.

activity.prompt: My freelance profile is ready when…
items: My headline states my niche and the benefit to clients
I have 3–6 portfolio pieces with problem, action and result
I have permission to show every piece
My services and starting prices are clear
My photo and contact details are professional
My name and style match across platforms

quiz.q: How many pieces should a focused portfolio show?
quiz.why: A focused portfolio shows your best 3–6 pieces. Quality matters more than quantity.
A strong headline names your niche and the benefit you give. Clients then see the value at once.

quiz.q: Using someone else's work in your portfolio is…
options: Dishonest and can get you banned
quiz.why: Putting someone else's work in your portfolio is dishonest and can get you banned. Never misrepresent work as yours.
Each portfolio piece should explain the problem, what you did and the result. This shows your thinking and the impact.

scenes.text: Sameer, a designer in Indore, charged ₹200 per logo to win clients. He worked 14-hour days and still couldn't pay rent.
A mentor helped him calculate a real rate from his monthly needs and billable hours.
He started sending proposals that showed understanding of the client's problem, with three package options.
Fewer clients, better pay, and he finally had weekends off.

steps.title: Calculate your minimum rate
steps.body:
1. Monthly money you need (living + savings + taxes + software/internet).
2. Realistic **billable hours** per month — not all working hours are billable (admin, learning, finding clients). Many freelancers bill around half their working time.
3. **Minimum hourly rate = monthly need ÷ billable hours.**

Example: need ₹40,000/month, 80 billable hours → minimum **₹500/hour**.

steps.title: Hourly, project and package pricing
steps.body:
- **Hourly**: fair for unclear scope; clients may worry about cost.
- **Project/fixed**: estimate hours × rate, add buffer for revisions.
- **Packages**: Basic / Standard / Premium — clients often choose the middle.

Always define **scope** (what's included), **revisions** (how many), and **timeline**.

steps.title: A proposal that wins
steps.body:
1. **Show you understood**: 'You need 10 Instagram posts a month for your bakery's new eggless range.'
2. **Your approach**: 'I'll create a consistent look, plan a content calendar, and write captions.'
3. **Proof**: one relevant sample link.
4. **Options and price**, timeline, revisions.
5. **Clear next step**: 'Shall we start with a 15-minute call on Tuesday?'

Keep it short and specific — generic copy-paste proposals are ignored.

steps.title: Underpricing hurts everyone
steps.body: Extremely low prices attract difficult clients, cause burnout, and make it hard to raise rates later. Compete on clarity, reliability and results.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Calculate your minimum hourly rate. Then write a 6-line proposal for an imaginary client in your niche.

activity.prompt: You need ₹45,000 a month and can bill 90 hours. What is your minimum hourly rate?

quiz.why: Minimum hourly rate = monthly income needed ÷ billable hours. This makes sure your real costs are covered.

quiz.q: Why define the number of revisions?
quiz.why: Defining the number of revisions avoids endless unpaid changes. A clear scope protects both sides.

options: Showing you understood the client's need
quiz.why: A strong proposal starts by showing you understood the client's need. Clients care about their problem, not about your life story.

options: Clients like a clear middle option
quiz.why: Packages work because clients like a clear middle option, so it is easier to decide. This is called choice architecture.

lessons.title: Contracts, payments, scams and tax

scenes.text: Meera, a translator in Chennai, got an email: 'We'll send ₹50,000 for a ₹20,000 job. Please refund the extra ₹30,000 to our agent.'
It felt too good. She checked online and found it's a well-known overpayment scam.
She declined, reported the account, and blocked it.
She now uses a simple written agreement and takes 50% advance from new clients.

steps.title: A simple agreement
steps.body:
Even a clear email can work as a basic agreement. Include:

- **Scope**: deliverables, formats, quantities.
- **Timeline** and milestones.
- **Price, payment terms** (e.g. 50% advance, 50% on delivery), and late-payment terms.
- **Revisions** included and the cost of extras.
- **Ownership/usage rights** after full payment.
- **Confidentiality** if needed.

Get the client's written 'yes' before starting.

steps.title: Scams to recognise
steps.body:
- **Pay-to-work**: registration fees, 'training kits', security deposits.
- **Task scams**: paid to like videos or write reviews, then asked to 'invest' to unlock bigger earnings.
- **Overpayment**: they 'pay' too much and ask you to refund the difference — the original payment bounces or is reversed.
- **Off-platform pressure**: moving to private chats to avoid platform protection.
- **OTP/PIN requests** or remote-access apps.

Report cyber fraud on **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: Getting paid
steps.body: Use reputable channels: platform payments, bank transfer, UPI for Indian clients, and established international payment services for foreign clients. Keep invoices and payment records. For foreign payments, keep the inward remittance documents your bank or payment provider issues — they help with tax and records.

steps.title: Tax basics in India (general awareness)
steps.body:
- Freelance income is **taxable income** — file your income tax return.
- Some professionals can use **presumptive taxation** schemes; whether you qualify depends on your profession and receipts.
- You may need to pay **advance tax** during the year if your tax liability crosses the threshold.
- **GST** registration may apply once service turnover crosses the threshold; exports of services have special GST treatment.

Rules change — consult a chartered accountant. This is general education, not tax advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a one-page agreement template for your niche covering scope, timeline, price, payment terms, revisions and rights.

statements.s: A client who overpays and asks you to refund the extra is a common scam pattern.
statements.why: The original payment often reverses later.

statements.s: Paying a registration fee is normal for genuine freelance work.
statements.why: Genuine clients pay you, not the other way round.

statements.s: A clear email confirming scope, price and timeline is better than no agreement.
statements.why: Written terms prevent disputes.

statements.s: Freelance income in India is tax-free.
statements.why: It is taxable; file returns and consult a CA.

statements.s: 1930 is India's cyber fraud helpline.
statements.why: Report quickly to improve chances of recovery.

quiz.q: A common payment term for new clients is…
quiz.why: A common term for new clients is 50% advance and 50% on delivery. It shares the risk fairly between you and the client.

quiz.q: 'Like videos, earn money, then invest to unlock more' is…
quiz.why: 'Like videos, earn money, then invest to unlock more' is a classic task scam. Real work never asks you to pay in to earn.

quiz.q: Who should you consult for freelance tax questions?
quiz.why: Tax rules depend on your situation, so ask a chartered accountant (CA) about freelance tax.
Ownership of the work usually transfers after full payment, as agreed in the contract. This protects you from non-payment.

sources: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre helpline 1930 (general awareness)

questions.q: Which is a genuine sign of a scam?
options: You're asked to pay to get work
questions.why: Being asked to pay to get work is a genuine sign of a scam. Real clients may ask for portfolios, timelines or a call.
A portfolio should have your best 3–6 relevant pieces. Showing everything or others' work is a mistake.

options: You stand out to specific clients
questions.why: A niche helps you stand out to specific clients. Specific positioning wins more than being general.
Minimum rate = ₹30,000 ÷ 60 billable hours = ₹500 per hour.
Scope in an agreement says which deliverables are included. It sets what work is and is not covered.

questions.q: Best way to report cyber fraud in India?
questions.why: Report cyber fraud in India by calling 1930 or using cybercrime.gov.in. These are the official channels.

questions.q: Why not count all working hours as billable?
options: Admin, learning and finding clients take time
questions.why: Not all working hours are billable, because admin, learning and finding clients also take time. Plan with realistic billable hours.

questions.q: A proposal is most likely to win when it…
options: Shows understanding of the client's specific need with one relevant sample
questions.why: A proposal wins when it shows you understood the client's specific need, and gives one relevant sample. Generic and long proposals are ignored.

questions.q: A client overpays ₹25,000 and asks for the extra back urgently. You should…
options: Suspect a scam, wait for funds to fully clear and verify; decline refunds to third parties
questions.why: An urgent request to return an overpayment is a classic scam. Wait until the funds fully clear, verify, and don't refund to third parties.

options: Leads to burnout, difficult clients and hard-to-raise rates
questions.why: Very low pricing leads to burnout and difficult clients, and it is hard to raise rates later. It isn't illegal, but it isn't sustainable.

questions.q: A client wants unlimited revisions for a fixed price. Best response?
options: Offer a set number of revisions and a rate for extras
questions.why: Offer a set number of revisions and a price for extras. This keeps the scope clear and the work paid.

questions.q: Which statement about freelance tax in India is most accurate?
options: It's taxable; presumptive schemes may apply to some professions; GST may apply above a threshold — consult a CA
questions.why: Freelance income is taxable. Presumptive schemes may apply to some professions, and GST may apply above a threshold. The rules depend on your case, so consult a CA.

courses.title: Kitchen gardening and farming basics
courses.summary: Grow vegetables and herbs on a balcony, terrace or plot: sunlight, soil and containers, seeds and Indian seasons, water, compost and natural pest control — and how farming works as a business with public support schemes.
outcomes: Learners can set up containers or beds with the right sun, soil mix and drainage
Learners can sow seeds correctly and match crops to Kharif, Rabi and Zaid seasons
Learners can water well, make compost and manage common pests naturally and safely
Learners can describe farming as a business and where farmers can get help

story.title: The balcony that fed a family

scenes.text: In a Mumbai flat, 11-year-old Aarav and his grandmother Sudha decided to grow vegetables on their balcony.
First they watched where sunlight fell: the east side got 6 hours of morning sun.
They drilled drainage holes in old buckets and mixed soil, compost and cocopeat.
Three months later they picked their first tomatoes and a basket of spinach.

steps.title: Sunlight decides what you can grow
steps.body:
- **6+ hours of direct sun**: fruiting vegetables — tomato, chilli, brinjal, okra (bhindi), beans, gourds.
- **3–5 hours**: leafy greens and herbs — spinach (palak), methi, coriander, mint, lettuce.
- **Less than 3 hours**: limited choice — try mint, some ornamental plants, or microgreens indoors near a bright window.

Watch your space for a day and note when it gets direct sun.

steps.title: Containers and drainage
steps.body:
- Any container works if it has **drainage holes** — buckets, paint tins, grow bags, crates lined with cloth.
- **Depth guide**: leafy greens and herbs 15–20 cm; chilli, brinjal, tomato 30 cm or more; gourds and climbers need large containers and support.
- Raise containers slightly so water can drain; check that terrace waterproofing is protected (use trays or a plastic sheet).

steps.title: A good potting mix
steps.body:
Plain garden soil packs hard in pots. A common home mix is roughly:

- **40% garden soil**
- **30% compost** (or well-rotted cow dung manure / vermicompost)
- **30% cocopeat** (holds moisture and keeps the mix light)

A little neem cake can be added. Good mix is loose, crumbly and drains well.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pots without drainage holes (roots rot), heavy clay soil only, placing sun-loving crops in shade, and overcrowding too many plants in one container.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Track sunlight on your balcony/terrace/window every two hours for one day. Decide whether you can grow fruiting vegetables or should start with leafy greens.

activity.label: Hours of direct sunlight your space gets

bands.text: Very little sun. Try mint, microgreens near a bright window, or shade-tolerant plants.
Good for leafy greens and herbs: spinach, methi, coriander, mint, lettuce.
Excellent for fruiting vegetables: tomato, chilli, brinjal, okra, beans and gourds — plus everything else.

quiz.q: Tomatoes and chillies need about how much direct sun?
quiz.why: Fruiting crops like tomatoes and chillies need 6 or more hours of direct sun a day.

quiz.q: Why must containers have drainage holes?
options: So roots don't sit in water and rot
quiz.why: Containers need drainage holes so excess water drains out. Roots sitting in water rot.

quiz.q: Why add cocopeat to a potting mix?
options: It holds moisture and keeps mix light
quiz.why: Cocopeat holds moisture and keeps the potting mix light and airy. It improves the texture.

quiz.q: Which grows better in partial sun?
quiz.why: Leafy greens like spinach tolerate partial sun. Brinjal, okra and watermelon need full sun.

story.title: Why the coriander didn't come up

scenes.text: Pooja in Ahmedabad sowed coriander seeds deep in May. Nothing grew.
Her neighbour, a retired agriculture officer, Mr. Desai, explained: coriander prefers cooler months, and seeds were sown too deep.
In October she gently crushed the seeds into halves, sowed them shallow, and kept the soil moist.
Tiny green shoots appeared within about two weeks.

steps.title: India's three cropping seasons
steps.body:
- **Kharif** (sown with the monsoon, about June–July; harvested about September–October): rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut, bajra, jowar.
- **Rabi** (sown about October–December; harvested about March–April): wheat, mustard, gram (chana), barley, peas.
- **Zaid** (short summer season between Rabi and Kharif, about March–June): watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, moong.

Exact timing varies by region and climate.

steps.title: Kitchen-garden calendar (general guide)
steps.body:
- **Cool season (roughly Oct–Feb in much of India)**: spinach, methi, coriander, radish, carrot, peas, cabbage, cauliflower, lettuce.
- **Warm/summer (roughly Feb–Jun)**: okra, gourds, cucumber, beans, amaranth (chaulai).
- **Monsoon**: many gourds, beans, brinjal and chilli transplants; avoid waterlogging.
- Tomato, chilli and brinjal can be grown much of the year in milder climates.

Local nurseries and Krishi Vigyan Kendras know the best timing for your area.

steps.title: How to sow
steps.body:
- **Depth**: about **2–3 times the seed's size**. Tiny seeds (lettuce) barely covered; big seeds (beans) deeper.
- Keep soil **moist, not soggy** until germination.
- **Direct sow** crops that dislike transplanting: radish, carrot, beans, peas, coriander, spinach.
- **Raise seedlings** in trays and transplant: tomato, chilli, brinjal, cabbage — transplant when they have a few true leaves, ideally in the evening, then water.
- Coriander seeds can be gently split into halves before sowing.

steps.title: Spacing and succession
steps.body: Give plants room — crowded plants compete for light and nutrients and get more disease. Sow small batches of leafy greens every 2–3 weeks (succession sowing) for a steady harvest.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Sow a few seeds of a fast crop (methi or spinach) in a small container this week. Note the date of sowing, germination and first harvest.

activity.prompt: Which season is each field crop mainly grown in?

quiz.why: Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon (June–July), because they depend on its rains.
Wheat is a rabi crop: it is sown in winter and harvested in spring.

quiz.q: How deep should seeds generally be sown?
quiz.why: Sow seeds at a depth of about 2–3 times their size. Too deep, and the seedling can't reach the surface.

quiz.q: Which is usually raised as seedlings and transplanted?
quiz.why: Tomato is usually raised as seedlings and then transplanted. Root crops like carrot and radish don't like their roots disturbed.

lessons.title: Water, compost and natural pest control

scenes.text: Thomas in Thrissur noticed tiny green insects clustering under his chilli leaves; the leaves curled.
His daughter looked it up: aphids. Their school garden teacher suggested a mild neem-oil spray in the evening.
They also spotted ladybirds — natural predators — and avoided harsh chemicals that would kill them too.
Within two weeks the plants recovered. Their kitchen scraps now go into a compost bin.

steps.title: Watering well
steps.body:
- **Finger test**: push a finger 2–3 cm into the soil; water when it feels dry at that depth.
- Water **deeply** at the base, preferably in the **early morning** (or evening), not on leaves in hot sun.
- Containers dry faster than ground beds, especially in summer — check daily.
- **Overwatering** is as harmful as underwatering: yellowing leaves and a sour smell can mean roots are waterlogged.
- **Mulch** (dry leaves, straw) on top keeps soil cool and moist.

steps.title: Making compost at home
steps.body:
Mix **greens** (vegetable peels, fruit scraps, tea leaves, fresh plant waste) with **browns** (dry leaves, shredded cardboard, sawdust) — roughly **1 part greens to 2–3 parts browns** by volume.

- Keep it as moist as a wrung-out sponge.
- Turn or mix every week or so for air.
- Avoid meat, fish, dairy and oily food in simple home bins — they smell and attract pests.
- In about 2–3 months (faster in warm weather), you get dark, earthy-smelling compost.

steps.title: Natural pest control
steps.body:
- **Inspect** under leaves weekly; remove affected leaves or pick off caterpillars by hand.
- **Spray water** to knock off aphids.
- **Neem oil spray**: a commonly used home recipe is about 5 ml neem oil plus a few drops of liquid soap (to mix) in 1 litre of water. Test on a few leaves first and spray in the **evening**.
- Encourage **friendly insects** (ladybirds, bees) by growing flowers like marigold and avoiding broad chemical sprays.
- Healthy soil and good spacing prevent many problems.

steps.title: If chemical pesticides are used
steps.body: Follow the label exactly, wear gloves/mask, keep children and pets away, never store in food containers, and respect the **waiting period before harvest** stated on the label. Ask the local agriculture department or KVK for advice before using any chemical.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Start a small compost bin from a bucket with holes. Track what you add for a month and how it changes.

activity.prompt: Green or brown compost material — or keep out of a home bin?

quiz.q: When should you water container plants?
options: When the top 2–3 cm is dry
quiz.why: Water container plants when the top 2–3 cm of soil is dry. The finger test avoids over- and under-watering.

quiz.q: Best time to spray neem oil?
quiz.why: Spray neem oil in the evening. This avoids leaf burn in the hot sun and protects pollinators like bees that are active by day.
A rough compost ratio is 1 part greens to 2–3 parts browns. The balance prevents smell and speeds up composting.
Ladybirds are helpful predators that eat aphids. They help protect your plants.

lessons.title: Farming as a business

scenes.text: Lakshmi farms two acres near Warangal. Yields were falling and fertiliser costs rising.
She got a free Soil Health Card test, which showed her soil needed less of one fertiliser and more organic matter.
At the Krishi Vigyan Kendra she learned drip irrigation and vegetable intercropping.
Her costs fell, water use dropped and her vegetable sales at the local market gave steady weekly income.

steps.title: Think like a farm business
steps.body:
- **Costs**: seeds, fertiliser, labour, water/electricity, machinery hire, transport, interest.
- **Revenue**: yield × price — and price depends on timing, quality and where you sell.
- **Profit** = revenue − costs. Keep simple records per crop and per season.
- **Diversify**: mix field crops, vegetables, dairy, poultry or horticulture to spread risk.

steps.title: Soil and water
steps.body:
- **Soil testing** tells you what nutrients your soil needs — avoid wasting money on fertiliser it doesn't need. The **Soil Health Card** scheme provides soil testing and recommendations.
- **Drip and sprinkler irrigation** deliver water efficiently and can save a lot of water compared with flood irrigation.
- Organic matter (compost, green manure, crop residue instead of burning) improves soil over time.

steps.title: Where farmers can get help (India)
steps.body:
- **Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs)**: district-level farm science centres offering training and demonstrations.
- **Kisan Call Centre**: toll-free **1800-180-1551** for farming queries in local languages.
- **PM-KISAN**: income support of ₹6,000 a year in three instalments to eligible farmer families.
- **Crop insurance** (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana) for eligible crops and farmers.
- **Kisan Credit Card** for short-term crop credit through banks.
- **Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs)** help small farmers buy inputs and sell produce together.

Check official portals for current eligibility.

steps.title: Selling better
steps.body: Grade and clean produce, sell at the right time, compare mandi and direct-to-customer options (local markets, housing societies, online platforms), and consider simple value addition — cleaning and packing, drying, pickles — after checking FSSAI rules for food products.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For one crop (real or imaginary), list all costs for a season and estimate yield and price. Calculate profit. What one change would improve it most?

activity.prompt: Match the support with what it does.
pairs: ₹6,000 a year income support to eligible farmer families
Efficient water delivery to plant roots

quiz.q: Why test soil before adding fertiliser?
options: To apply only what the soil needs and save money
quiz.why: A soil test shows what the soil needs, so you apply only that. It saves money and protects the soil.
PM-KISAN gives eligible farmer families ₹6,000 a year, paid in three instalments. It is an income support scheme.

quiz.q: A benefit of drip irrigation is…
quiz.why: Drip irrigation delivers water efficiently to the roots, so less is wasted.
Profit = revenue − costs. If costs are bigger, it is a loss.

sources: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare schemes (general awareness)
ICAR Krishi Vigyan Kendras

questions.why: Pots must have drainage holes. Without them water collects and the roots rot.

questions.q: Which crop needs the most sun?
questions.why: Tomato is a fruiting crop that needs 6 or more hours of sun. Leafy crops and microgreens manage with less.
Rice is mainly a kharif crop, sown with the monsoon.

questions.q: Seeds are generally sown at a depth of…
questions.why: Seeds are generally sown at 2–3 times their own size. Deeper seeds struggle to emerge.

questions.q: Which should NOT go into a simple home compost bin?
questions.why: Meat and dairy should not go in a simple home compost bin, because they smell and attract pests. Peels, tea leaves and dry leaves are fine.
Mulch is a layer over the soil. It keeps the soil cool and moist, and reduces weeds.

questions.q: Yellow leaves and sour-smelling soil in a pot often mean…
questions.why: Yellow leaves and sour-smelling soil often mean overwatering. The roots are waterlogged and starting to rot.
Mustard and gram are rabi crops, sown in winter.

questions.q: Why spray neem oil in the evening?
options: Avoid leaf burn and protect bees
questions.why: Neem oil is best sprayed in the evening. This avoids leaf burn and protects bees, which are active during the day.

questions.q: Which crop dislikes transplanting and is best direct-sown?
questions.why: Carrot is a root crop that dislikes transplanting, so it is direct-sown. Tomato, chilli and brinjal are normally transplanted.

questions.q: A farmer wants local-language advice by phone. Best option?
questions.why: The Kisan Call Centre (1800-180-1551) is the dedicated farm helpline for advice, including in local languages.

questions.q: Revenue ₹1,20,000, costs ₹85,000. Profit and a key improvement idea?
options: ₹35,000; e.g. soil testing to cut unneeded fertiliser
questions.why: Profit = 1,20,000 − 85,000 = ₹35,000. Soil testing can cut costs by avoiding fertiliser that isn't needed.

trades-creative-service.title: Hunar: Tailoring, beauty & food trades
trades-creative-service.description: Skills you can earn from at home or in a shop — tailoring, beauty and grooming, and cooking and baking as a career — with hygiene, pricing and customer care built in. Continued in 'Hunar: Shop, freelance & farm'.

courses.title: Tailoring and stitching from scratch
courses.summary: Learn tools, fabrics and grain, take accurate body measurements, run and troubleshoot a sewing machine, and price and run a small tailoring business.
outcomes: Learners can choose fabric and understand grain, shrinkage and seam allowance
Learners can take and record standard body measurements accurately
Learners can thread, set up and troubleshoot a sewing machine
Learners can price a garment and run a small tailoring business

scenes.text: Shabana in Aligarh stitched her first kurta. After one wash, the side seams twisted towards the front.
Her neighbour, master tailor Iqbal chacha, laughed kindly: 'You cut it off-grain, and you didn't pre-wash the cotton.'
He showed her the selvedge, how to fold fabric along the grain, and to soak cotton before cutting.
Her next kurta hung straight. 'Fabric has a direction,' she wrote in her notebook.

steps.title: Your starter toolkit
steps.body:
- **Measuring tape** (cm and inches) and a **scale / L-square**
- **Fabric scissors** used only for fabric (paper blunts them) and small **thread snips**
- **Tailor's chalk** or fabric marker
- **Pins, pin cushion, hand needles**, a **seam ripper**
- **Sewing machine** (hand, treadle or electric) with spare needles and bobbins
- An **iron** — pressing as you sew is half of a professional finish

steps.title: Know your fabric
steps.body:
- **Cotton**: breathable, easy to sew, may shrink — **pre-wash or soak before cutting**.
- **Rayon/viscose**: drapes well, slippery, can shrink; handle gently.
- **Polyester and blends**: little shrinkage, less breathable, press at lower heat.
- **Silk**: delicate; sharp fine needle, low heat.
- **Denim/canvas**: heavy; needs a thicker needle.

Always test the iron heat and wash behaviour on a small scrap first.

steps.title: Grain, selvedge and seam allowance
steps.body:
- The **selvedge** is the finished edge of the fabric that doesn't fray.
- **Lengthwise grain** runs parallel to the selvedge — the strongest, least stretchy direction. Most garment pieces are cut with their length along it.
- **Crosswise grain** runs selvedge to selvedge; **bias** is at 45° and stretches the most — used for piping and bias binding.
- **Seam allowance** is the extra fabric between the cutting line and the stitching line — commonly about **1–1.5 cm** (many tailors leave more at side seams to allow later alteration).

steps.title: Common beginner mistakes
steps.body:
- Cutting cotton without pre-washing → garment shrinks.
- Cutting off-grain → seams twist after washing.
- Forgetting seam allowance → garment too tight.
- Using paper scissors on fabric → chewed edges.
- Skipping pressing → bumpy, home-made look.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take a piece of cotton. Find the selvedge. Pull gently along the lengthwise grain, crosswise grain and the bias. Which stretches most? Soak a 10 × 10 cm square, dry and iron it, and measure the shrinkage.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Extra fabric beyond the stitch line

quiz.why: The bias (45° to the grain) stretches the most. That's why bias strips are used for binding curves.

options: So it shrinks before cutting, not after stitching
quiz.why: Cotton often shrinks on its first wash. Pre-washing means it shrinks before you cut, not after you've stitched.

quiz.q: A common seam allowance is about…
quiz.why: A common seam allowance is about 1–1.5 cm. This is the extra fabric beyond the stitching line.
Keep fabric scissors only for fabric. Cutting paper blunts the blades, and then they won't cut cloth cleanly.

scenes.text: Lata runs a small boutique in Nashik. A bride's blouse came back too tight at the armhole.
Lata realised her helper had measured over a thick sweater and pulled the tape tight.
She trained her helper: measure over light clothing, keep the tape snug not tight, keep it level, and write each number immediately.
Fitting complaints dropped sharply, and the bride sent two cousins to the boutique.

steps.title: Rules for accurate measurement
steps.body:
- Measure over **light, well-fitting clothing**.
- Keep the tape **level** around the body and **snug, not tight** — you should be able to slip a finger under it.
- Ask the person to stand naturally, breathing normally, arms relaxed.
- Write each measurement **immediately**, with the customer's name, date and phone number.
- Measure twice if unsure; ask about preferred fit (loose, regular, fitted).

steps.title: Key measurements
steps.body:
- **Bust/Chest**: around the fullest part, tape level under the arms.
- **Waist**: around the natural waist (usually the narrowest part).
- **Hip**: around the fullest part of the seat.
- **Shoulder**: from one shoulder point to the other across the back.
- **Armhole**: around the arm where it joins the shoulder.
- **Sleeve length**: from shoulder point to the desired length.
- **Garment length**: e.g. for a kurta, from the highest point of the shoulder to the desired hem.
- **Neck** (for collars) and **round of upper arm** (for fitted sleeves).

steps.title: Ease: why clothes are bigger than the body
steps.body: Clothes need **ease** — extra room to breathe, sit and move. A fitted blouse might have a little ease at the bust; a relaxed kurta needs much more. Beginners often stitch exactly to body measurement, and the garment feels tight. Follow your pattern's ease or ask an experienced tailor until you know it by feel.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A customer's hip is 96 cm. For a straight kurta, you decide on 8 cm of ease → finished hip 104 cm. The kurta has a front and back piece, so each piece is 52 cm at the hip, and each half-piece (if cut on a fold) is 26 cm, **plus seam allowance** at the side seams (e.g. 1.5 cm) → mark 27.5 cm from the fold.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With permission, measure a family member and record all key measurements on a card. Measure again the next day — how close were you? Differences of more than 1 cm show where your technique needs work.

activity.prompt: Hip is 100 cm. You add 8 cm ease and cut the front piece on a fold (so you mark a quarter of the finished hip from the fold). Add 1.5 cm seam allowance. How far from the fold do you mark?

quiz.q: How tight should the tape be?
options: Snug, with a finger able to slip under
quiz.why: The tape should be snug, so a finger can slip under it. Too tight squeezes the body, and too loose gives wrong numbers.
The waist is measured at the natural waist, the narrowest part of the torso.

options: Extra room added for comfort and movement
quiz.why: Ease is extra room added to the body measurement for comfort and movement. Without it a garment would be too tight to wear.

quiz.q: Why record the date with measurements?
options: Bodies change; you know how current they are
quiz.why: Bodies change over time, so write the date with the measurements. Then you know how current they are.

story.title: The bird's nest under the fabric

scenes.text: Komal, 16, in Surat starts stitching a pillow cover. Underneath, the thread bunches into a messy tangle.
She changes the bobbin twice. Same problem.
Her grandmother lifts the presser foot, re-threads the top thread properly, and the stitches come out perfect.
'A tangle underneath is usually a problem on top,' says Dadi.

steps.title: Threading basics
steps.body:
- **Raise the presser foot** before threading the upper thread — this opens the tension discs so the thread seats properly.
- Follow the numbered path: spool → thread guide → tension discs → take-up lever → needle guides → needle (front to back on most machines).
- Wind the **bobbin** evenly and insert it in the direction the manual shows.
- Pull up the bobbin thread by turning the hand-wheel **towards you**.
- Use the same thread type on top and in the bobbin.

steps.title: Needles and stitch settings
steps.body:
- Needle sizes: lower numbers for fine fabric, higher for heavy — e.g. **70/10–80/12** for light cottons and silk, **90/14** for medium, **100/16** for denim/canvas.
- Change needles regularly; a blunt or bent needle causes skipped stitches and pulls.
- A typical straight stitch length is about **2.5 mm**; longer for basting/topstitching.
- **Backstitch** a few stitches at the start and end of seams to lock them.

steps.title: Troubleshooting chart
steps.body:
- **Tangle (bird's nest) under the fabric** → upper thread not in tension discs; re-thread with presser foot up.
- **Skipped stitches** → wrong, blunt or bent needle, or needle inserted wrong way.
- **Thread keeps breaking** → poor-quality thread, tension too tight, burr on needle, wrong threading.
- **Puckered seams** → tension too tight, stitch too long for fine fabric, pulling fabric.
- **Fabric not moving** → feed dogs lowered or presser foot not down.

steps.title: Hand stitches you still need
steps.body:
- **Running stitch** — basting and gathering.
- **Backstitch** — strong hand seam.
- **Hemming / slip stitch** — near-invisible hems.
- **Buttonhole stitch** and sewing on buttons with a thread shank.
- **Overcast** — stops raw edges fraying when there's no overlock machine.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Keep fingers away from the needle; don't sew over pins; unplug electric machines before changing needles or cleaning; oil the machine as the manual says and clean lint from the bobbin area regularly.

a.text: Your seam shows a big tangle of thread underneath. What do you check first?

choices.label: Replace the bobbin case
choices.feedback: A tangle underneath is usually caused by the upper thread.

choices.label: Re-thread the upper thread with the presser foot raised
choices.feedback: Right — that seats the thread in the tension discs.

b.text: The tangle is gone, but now the machine skips stitches on denim.

choices.label: Switch to a 100/16 needle, inserted correctly
choices.feedback: Heavy fabric needs a thicker, sharp needle.

choices.label: Push the fabric through faster
choices.feedback: Forcing fabric bends needles and can break them.

x1.text: The tangle continues. Most nests under the fabric come from upper threading — try re-threading next time.

x2.text: The needle bends and snaps. Always match the needle to the fabric, and let the feed dogs move the cloth.

good.text: Neat, even stitches on denim. You diagnosed like a tailor.

quiz.q: Why raise the presser foot when threading?
options: It opens the tension discs so the thread seats properly
quiz.why: Raising the presser foot opens the tension discs so the thread seats in them properly. Threading with the foot down is a classic cause of tangles.
Denim is heavy, so it needs a thicker needle such as 100/16. A thin needle bends or breaks.
Skipped stitches often come from the wrong, blunt or bent needle. Change the needle first.
Backstitching at the ends of a seam locks it, so the stitches don't unravel.

lessons.title: Pricing and running a tailoring business

story.title: From one machine to a shop

scenes.text: Parveen in Kanpur started stitching blouses at home, charging whatever neighbours offered.
At a women's self-help group meeting, she learned to calculate her real cost: thread, lining, electricity, and her hours.
She set fixed prices, gave delivery dates in writing, and kept a measurement register.
Two years later she runs a small shop with two helpers and registered her business under Udyam.

steps.title: Price = materials + time + overheads + profit
steps.body:
- **Materials** you supply: lining, thread, buttons, hooks, fall/pico, interfacing.
- **Time**: hours × your hourly rate (decide what an hour of skilled work is worth locally).
- **Overheads**: electricity, rent, machine maintenance, needles, phone, transport — spread across jobs.
- **Profit margin**: so you can grow, save and survive slow months.

steps.title: Worked example: a lined blouse
steps.body:
- Materials: ₹60 (lining, hooks, thread)
- Time: 2.5 hours × ₹100/hour = ₹250
- Overheads share: ₹30
- Subtotal: ₹340; add 20% profit → **₹408**, so you might price it at ₹400–450 depending on local rates and design complexity.

Charge extra for designer necklines, embroidery, urgent delivery, and alterations by type.

steps.title: Systems that build a reputation
steps.body:
- A **measurement register** (book or phone) per customer.
- An **order slip** with design, price, advance paid, delivery date — give a copy.
- Take an **advance** (commonly 30–50%) for custom work.
- Keep fabric labelled with the customer's name.
- Photograph finished pieces (with permission) for a portfolio on WhatsApp/Instagram.

steps.title: Support for small businesses
steps.body:
- **Udyam registration** (free, online) records your business as a micro/small enterprise.
- **PM Mudra Yojana** offers collateral-free small business loans through banks for eligible micro-enterprises.
- Self-help groups and skill-training centres run tailoring courses; some schemes support women entrepreneurs. Check official portals for current eligibility.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Price three items you could make (a cotton kurta, a lined blouse, a pillow cover) using the formula. Compare with two local tailors' prices and decide where you sit.

activity.prompt: Complete the pricing formula and rules.
activity.text: Price = materials + ___ + overheads + ___. For custom orders, take an ___ before cutting.

quiz.why: Overheads are shared running costs, like electricity and machine maintenance. They're not tied to one order, unlike buttons, lining or the customer's fabric.

quiz.q: Why take an advance on custom work?
options: It covers materials and reduces risk of abandoned orders
quiz.why: An advance covers the cost of materials and reduces the risk of abandoned custom orders. It protects your time and money.

quiz.q: Materials ₹50, time 2 h at ₹120/h, overheads ₹30, profit 20%. Price?

options: A paid licence for factories only
A free online registration for micro/small enterprises
quiz.why: Udyam registration is a free online registration for micro and small enterprises. It is not a tax or a loan.

options: The finished, non-fraying edge of fabric
questions.why: The selvedge is the finished edge of the fabric, which doesn't fray.
A seam ripper cuts and removes wrong stitches safely.

options: At the fullest part, tape level
questions.why: Measure the bust or chest at the fullest part, with the tape held level around the body.
Pre-washing cotton prevents shrinkage after stitching. Shrink the fabric first, then cut it.
A typical straight-stitch length is about 2.5 mm.
Bias strips stretch, so they are used for piping and for binding curves.

questions.q: Thread bunching under the fabric is usually caused by…
options: Upper thread not seated in tension discs
questions.why: Thread bunching under the fabric usually means the upper thread wasn't seated in the tension discs. Re-thread with the presser foot up.

options: So the garment allows breathing and movement
questions.why: Ease is added so the garment allows breathing and movement. Without it, the garment would be uncomfortably tight.

questions.q: A kurta cut off-grain will likely…
options: Twist at the seams after washing
questions.why: A kurta cut off-grain tends to twist at the seams after washing. Cutting along the grain gives a good hang.

questions.q: Hip 92 cm, ease 8 cm, cut on fold (quarter of finished hip) + 1.5 cm seam allowance. Mark at…
questions.why: Finished hip = 92 + 8 = 100 cm. Cut on the fold you draft a quarter: 100 ÷ 4 = 25 cm, then add the 1.5 cm seam allowance to mark at 26.5 cm.

questions.q: Puckered seams on fine fabric suggest…
options: Tension too tight or stitch too long
questions.why: Puckered seams on fine fabric usually mean the tension is too tight or the stitch is too long. Reduce the tension or shorten the stitch.

questions.q: Materials ₹80, time 3 h at ₹100, overheads ₹40, 25% profit. Price?

courses.title: Beauty and grooming: skills and safe practice
courses.summary: Hygiene and client safety first, then skin and hair basics, common services with their precautions, men's grooming, client consultation and building a beauty career.
outcomes: Learners can apply salon hygiene: clean, disinfect, single-use items, no double-dipping
Learners can identify skin types and explain basic skin and hair care
Learners can run a client consultation including patch tests and contraindications
Learners can plan a career path and price services

scenes.text: A customer at a small parlour in Guwahati developed an infected cuticle after a manicure.
The owner, Bornali, traced it: the same metal pusher had been used on three clients and only wiped with a towel.
She set up a system: clean, disinfect, dry and store tools in closed containers; single-use files and wax spatulas.
She displayed her hygiene steps on the wall. Clients started choosing her parlour because of it.

steps.title: Clean → disinfect → store
steps.body:
- **Clean**: wash tools with soap/detergent and water to remove hair, skin and product.
- **Disinfect**: immerse in or apply a suitable disinfectant for the contact time on the label; some salons also use autoclaves or other sterilisers for metal tools.
- **Dry and store** in a clean, closed container.
- Wash hands before and after every client.
- Clean towels and capes for each client; launder at high temperature.

steps.title: Single-use and no double-dipping
steps.body:
- Single-use items: wax spatulas, cotton, disposable razors and blades, nail files and buffers that can't be disinfected, threading thread.
- **Never double-dip** a used spatula into wax or a used applicator into product — scoop with a clean spatula into a bowl.
- Never reuse a blade on another client.

steps.title: When not to do a service
steps.body: Do not work on skin that is **broken, infected, sunburnt, has open sores or active rashes**. Clients using certain acne medicines (such as oral isotretinoin or retinoid creams) can have fragile skin that tears with waxing — ask before waxing. When in doubt, refer the client to a doctor or dermatologist. You are a beauty professional, not a medical one.

steps.title: Product safety
steps.body:
- Store products closed, away from heat and sunlight; check expiry dates.
- Read labels for ventilation and glove advice (e.g. hair colour, nail products).
- Test wax temperature on your own inner wrist before applying.
- Keep a first-aid kit; know how to handle a small cut or burn.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a hygiene checklist poster for a small parlour: before each client, during, after. Keep it to 8 clear lines.

activity.prompt: Reusable after cleaning and disinfecting, or single-use?

quiz.why: Clean first to remove debris, then disinfect, then dry and store. Disinfectant doesn't work well on dirty tools.

quiz.q: Double-dipping a used spatula into wax…
quiz.why: Double-dipping a used spatula contaminates the whole pot of wax, and can spread infection between clients.

quiz.q: Client has sunburnt skin and wants waxing. You…
quiz.why: Sunburnt skin is damaged, so waxing is not safe. Postpone the service until the skin has healed.

quiz.q: Where do you test wax temperature?
quiz.why: Test wax temperature on your own inner wrist, never on the client first. This protects them from burns.

scenes.text: Riya, 19, in Delhi bought every product she saw online. Her skin became red and broke out.
Her cousin Nandini, a trained beautician, asked about her skin type and routine.
They simplified: gentle cleanser, moisturiser, sunscreen by day; one new product at a time with a patch test.
In a few weeks her skin calmed. 'Simple and consistent beats many and random,' said Nandini.

steps.title: Skin types
steps.body:
- **Normal**: balanced, few issues.
- **Dry**: feels tight, may flake — needs richer moisturiser, gentle cleansing.
- **Oily**: shine, enlarged pores, prone to breakouts — light, non-comedogenic products.
- **Combination**: oily T-zone (forehead, nose, chin), drier cheeks.
- **Sensitive**: reacts easily — fragrance-free, minimal products, patch test everything.

Skin type can change with age, climate and hormones.

steps.title: The basic routine
steps.body:
1. **Cleanse** gently (twice a day; avoid harsh scrubbing).
2. **Moisturise** suited to skin type.
3. **Sunscreen** in the day — broad-spectrum, commonly SPF 30 or more, reapplied when outdoors for long periods.

Introduce **one new product at a time** and patch test first. Persistent acne, sudden pigmentation, moles that change, or rashes need a **dermatologist**.

steps.title: Hair basics
steps.body:
- Hair types range from straight to wavy, curly and coily; scalp can be oily, dry or normal.
- Shampoo cleans the **scalp**; conditioner smooths the **lengths**.
- Heat tools (straighteners, dryers) damage hair — use heat protectant and moderate temperatures.
- Some hair fall daily is normal; **sudden or patchy hair loss** should be checked by a doctor.
- Dandruff often responds to medicated shampoos; persistent scalp problems need medical advice.

steps.title: Men's grooming essentials
steps.body:
- **Shaving**: soften the beard with warm water, use a sharp blade and shaving cream/gel, shave **with the direction of hair growth** first to reduce irritation and ingrown hairs, rinse with cool water, moisturise.
- **Beard care**: trim regularly, shape the neckline, wash and condition the beard.
- Skin basics are the same for everyone: cleanse, moisturise, sunscreen.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: At midday, gently press a tissue on your forehead, nose, cheeks and chin. Where is it oily? Decide your skin type and write a simple 3-step routine.

cards.back: Combination skin
Dry skin — richer moisturiser, gentle cleanser
Sensitive skin — fragrance-free, patch test
Cleanse, moisturise, sunscreen (day)
With the direction of hair growth first
See a doctor

quiz.q: Which is the core daytime step many people skip?
quiz.why: Sunscreen is the daytime step many people skip. It protects the skin from sun damage.

quiz.q: How should new products be introduced?
options: One at a time with a patch test
quiz.why: Introduce new products one at a time with a patch test. That way you can tell which product causes a reaction.
Shampoo is mainly for cleaning the scalp. Conditioner is for the lengths of the hair.

quiz.q: A mole that changes shape or colour should be…
quiz.why: A mole that changes shape or colour should be checked by a doctor. Changing moles need medical review.

story.title: The patch test that saved a wedding

scenes.text: Two weeks before her wedding in Indore, Anjali wanted her hair coloured at Meera's salon.
Meera insisted on a patch test 48 hours before, as the dye maker's instructions say.
Anjali's skin reacted. Meera suggested a different approach and a doctor's advice.
'If you'd coloured my hair that day, I might have spent my wedding in hospital,' Anjali said.

steps.title: The consultation
steps.body:
Before any service, ask and record:

- What result do you want? (Show pictures.)
- Allergies, skin conditions, medicines (including acne treatments), pregnancy (for some treatments), recent sunburn.
- Previous chemical treatments (colour, straightening).
- Budget and time.

Then explain what is realistic, the price, the time, and aftercare. Get agreement before starting.

steps.title: Patch tests
steps.body: Many hair dyes contain ingredients (such as PPD) that can cause serious allergic reactions. Dye manufacturers typically instruct a **skin allergy test 48 hours before every colouring service**, even for regular clients — follow the product's instructions exactly. Record the date and result. If there is a reaction, **do not colour** and advise the client to see a doctor.

steps.title: Common services and their key precautions
steps.body:
- **Threading**: clean thread per client; stretch skin gently; avoid active acne or broken skin.
- **Waxing**: test temperature; apply in the direction of hair growth and remove against it (for soft wax with strips); support the skin; avoid broken/sunburnt skin.
- **Facials and clean-ups**: choose products by skin type; no harsh extraction on inflamed acne.
- **Manicure/pedicure**: never cut living skin aggressively; disinfect tools; check for fungal infections.
- **Bridal and party makeup**: skin prep, colour matching in daylight, hygienic applicators.

steps.title: Handling unrealistic expectations
steps.body: If a client with very dark hair wants pale blonde in one sitting, explain honestly that it may need several sessions and could damage hair. Offer options. Honest advice builds long-term trust far more than a risky 'yes'.

steps.title: If something goes wrong
steps.body: Stop the service, rinse with cool water if it's a product reaction, stay calm, record what happened, and advise medical help when needed (call **112** for severe reactions like swelling of the face or difficulty breathing).

a.text: A regular client wants her usual hair colour today. Her last patch test was six months ago. She's in a hurry.

choices.label: Skip the test — she's had it before
choices.feedback: Allergies can develop at any time; manufacturers advise testing before each service.

choices.label: Explain the 48-hour patch test and book her colour for later

b.text: She agrees. Meanwhile, she asks for waxing and mentions she started an acne cream with a retinoid last week.

choices.label: Wax as usual
choices.feedback: Retinoid-treated skin can lift and tear with waxing.

choices.label: Explain the risk, avoid waxing the treated area, offer an alternative

e1.text: Her scalp swells painfully after colouring. She needs medical care. Always follow the patch-test instructions.

e2.text: The skin lifts and becomes raw. Always ask about medicines and avoid waxing treated skin.

e3.text: She thanks you for caring. Her patch test is clear and she returns for colour two days later — and refers her sister.

quiz.q: When is a hair-dye patch test typically required by manufacturers?
quiz.why: Manufacturers typically require a patch test 48 hours before every colouring service. Allergies can develop at any time, even if there was no earlier reaction.

quiz.q: Which question belongs in a consultation?
quiz.why: Ask about allergies and medicines in a consultation, as health information affects safety. Caste, salary or exam marks are irrelevant and intrusive.

quiz.q: Client's face swells and breathing is difficult after a product. You…
quiz.why: A swollen face and difficulty breathing may be a severe allergic reaction. Stop and call 112 immediately.

quiz.q: For soft wax with strips, hair is removed…
quiz.why: With soft wax and strips, you apply with the hair growth and pull off against it. This removes the hair from the root.

scenes.text: Divya from Coimbatore started with home-service threading and waxing on her scooter.
She photographed bridal looks (with permission), collected reviews, and took a certified makeup course.
She used a simple booking calendar and kept client records: skin type, patch tests, preferences.
Within three years she opened a small studio and trains two juniors.

steps.title: Career paths
steps.body:
- Salon stylist, beautician, makeup artist (bridal, fashion, film/TV), nail technician, spa therapist, barber, trainer/educator, product sales and brand education, salon manager or owner.
- Training: short certificate courses, skill-council aligned programmes, brand academies, and apprenticeships in established salons. The Beauty & Wellness Sector Skill Council works on industry-recognised training standards in India.

steps.title: Pricing services
steps.body: Price = product cost per service + your time + overheads (rent, electricity, laundry, disposables, travel for home service) + profit. Check local competitors, then position yourself on quality, hygiene and reliability rather than being the cheapest. Package offers (e.g. bridal + pre-bridal) help planning.

steps.title: Marketing honestly
steps.body:
- Show **real** work; avoid heavy filters that mislead.
- Ask permission before posting any client photo.
- Collect reviews; respond politely to complaints.
- Be punctual; confirm bookings a day ahead.
- Keep client data private.

steps.title: Personal safety for home-service professionals
steps.body: Share your booking location and timings with a trusted person, confirm new clients by phone, carry a charged phone, and leave if you feel unsafe. Platforms and reputable salons often have safety protocols — use them.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a one-page plan: services you'll offer, prices, target customers, hygiene promise, and how you'll get your first 20 clients.

activity.prompt: Before launching my beauty service, I will…
items: Set up a written hygiene routine and single-use supplies
Prepare a consultation and patch-test record card
Calculate prices including products, time, overheads and profit
Build a portfolio of real work with client permission
Set a personal safety routine for home visits

quiz.q: Which is a good way to stand out?
quiz.why: Quality, hygiene and reliability build trust and bring repeat clients. Fake reviews or heavy filters mislead people.

quiz.q: Before posting a client's photo you must…
quiz.why: Get the client's permission before posting their photo. This respects their consent and privacy.

options: Share booking details with a trusted person
Never tell anyone where you go
Accept all unknown bookings late at night
quiz.why: For home services, share booking details with a trusted person, so someone knows where you are. Switching off your phone or accepting unknown late bookings is unsafe.
Service pricing should include products, your time, overheads and profit. If any is left out, you lose money.

questions.why: Wax spatulas should be single-use with no double-dipping. This prevents cross-contamination between clients.

questions.q: The basic daytime skin routine is…
questions.why: A basic daytime skin routine is cleanse, moisturise and sunscreen. Simple, consistent care works.

questions.q: Where do you test wax temperature?
questions.why: Test wax temperature on your own inner wrist to avoid burning the client.

questions.q: Oily T-zone with dry cheeks is…
questions.why: An oily T-zone with dry cheeks is combination skin, which has mixed zones.

options: Cleaned, then disinfected, then stored dry
questions.why: Clean tools first, then disinfect them, then store them dry. Disinfectant doesn't work well on dirty tools.

questions.q: Shaving with the direction of hair growth first helps…
questions.why: Shaving with the direction of hair growth first reduces irritation and the risk of ingrown hairs.

questions.q: Which is a contraindication for waxing?
questions.why: Sunburnt or broken skin is a contraindication for waxing, as the skin can be injured or torn.

questions.q: Hair-dye patch tests are typically done…
questions.why: Manufacturers usually ask for a hair-dye patch test about 48 hours before, because reactions can take time to appear.

questions.q: Client mentions oral isotretinoin. Best response?
options: Avoid waxing and advise checking with their doctor
questions.why: Oral isotretinoin can make skin fragile, so waxing could tear it. Avoid waxing and advise the client to check with their doctor.

questions.q: A client wants a drastic colour change in one sitting. Professional response?
options: Explain realistic steps, risks and options
questions.why: Explain realistic steps, risks and options for a drastic colour change. Promising it or using the strongest bleach can damage the hair and lose trust.

questions.q: A persistent rash on a client's face should be…
questions.why: A persistent rash needs medical care, so refer the client to a dermatologist. Beauticians don't treat medical conditions.

questions.q: Which pricing approach is most sustainable?
options: Give everything free to start forever
Calculate costs plus profit, then position on quality
questions.why: The sustainable way to price is to calculate costs plus profit and then position on quality. Copying the cheapest or charging randomly can lose money.

courses.title: Cooking and baking as a career
courses.summary: Food safety, kitchen roles and cooking methods, the science of baking, and costing and registering a home bakery or food business in India.
outcomes: Learners can apply food safety: temperature danger zone, cross-contamination, hygiene, allergens
Learners can describe kitchen roles and choose dry-heat or moist-heat methods
Learners can explain gluten, yeast and leaveners and use baker's percentages
Learners can cost a recipe, price it and know the FSSAI registration basics

lessons.title: Food safety comes first

scenes.text: After a big family function in Hyderabad, caterer Yusuf's helper left a large pot of biryani out overnight to cool.
Some guests who took leftovers home fell ill the next day.
Yusuf attended a food-safety training and learned about the temperature danger zone and rapid cooling.
Now his team spreads hot food into shallow trays and refrigerates within two hours. No more complaints.

steps.title: The temperature danger zone
steps.body:
Bacteria multiply fastest between about **5 °C and 60 °C**.

- Keep **cold food cold** (fridge at about 5 °C or below) and **hot food hot** (above 60 °C).
- Don't leave cooked food at room temperature for more than about **2 hours** (less in hot weather).
- **Cool quickly**: divide large quantities into shallow containers before refrigerating.
- **Reheat** until steaming hot throughout (core about 75 °C), and reheat only once.

steps.title: Cross-contamination
steps.body:
- Use **separate boards and knives** for raw meat/fish and ready-to-eat foods (salads, cooked food). Colour-coded boards help.
- Store raw meat **below** cooked food in the fridge so juices can't drip onto it.
- Wash hands with soap for at least **20 seconds** after handling raw meat, eggs, waste, or using the toilet.
- Clean and sanitise surfaces between tasks.

steps.title: Allergens
steps.body: Common food allergens include **peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat (gluten), soy, fish, shellfish and sesame**. Reactions can be life-threatening. Always know what is in each dish, tell customers honestly, prevent cross-contact (clean utensils), and label packaged food. If a customer has trouble breathing or swelling after eating, call **112**.

steps.title: Personal hygiene
steps.body: Clean uniform/apron, hair covered, nails short, no jewellery on hands, cover cuts with a waterproof plaster, and do not handle food when you have vomiting, diarrhoea or fever. Taste with a clean spoon each time — never the stirring spoon.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check your home fridge with a thermometer if you have one. Reorganise it: ready-to-eat on top shelves, raw meat/fish at the bottom in a covered container.

statements.s: Bacteria grow fastest between about 5 °C and 60 °C.
statements.why: That is the temperature danger zone.

statements.s: It's safe to cool a large pot of rice overnight on the counter.
statements.why: Large pots cool slowly; spread into shallow trays and refrigerate within about 2 hours.

statements.s: Raw meat should be stored below cooked food in the fridge.
statements.why: Prevents drips contaminating ready-to-eat food.

statements.s: You can use the same board for raw chicken and salad if you wipe it with a cloth.
statements.why: Wash and sanitise, or better, use separate boards.
