statements.s: Sesame and peanuts are common allergens.
statements.why: Always declare allergens.

quiz.q: Maximum time cooked food should sit at room temperature is about…
quiz.why: Cooked food should sit at room temperature for no more than about 2 hours, and less in hot weather. Bacteria multiply quickly at room temperature.

quiz.q: Best way to cool a big pot of dal quickly?
options: Divide into shallow containers, then refrigerate
Leave it covered on the stove
quiz.why: Divide a big pot of dal into shallow containers, then refrigerate. Shallow containers cool faster, so the food spends less time in the danger zone.

quiz.q: How long should you wash hands with soap?
quiz.why: Wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds. That is the standard guidance for removing germs.

quiz.q: A customer's lips swell after eating. You…
quiz.why: Swelling of the lips after eating may be a severe allergic reaction. Call 112 immediately.

sources: FSSAI food safety training (general awareness)
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food

story.title: First week in a hotel kitchen

scenes.text: Joseph, 20, joins a hotel kitchen in Kochi as a commis after a hospitality diploma.
He spends his first week peeling, chopping and learning mise en place — everything in its place before service.
The chef de partie teaches him why fish is poached gently but chicken tikka goes into a fierce tandoor.
By the month's end, Joseph runs the garnish station during dinner rush.

steps.title: The kitchen brigade
steps.body:
Large professional kitchens follow a hierarchy:

- **Executive chef** — menus, costs, team.
- **Sous chef** — second in command, runs daily operations.
- **Chef de partie** — in charge of a section (curries, tandoor, grill, pastry, cold kitchen).
- **Commis** — junior cooks who prep and assist.
- Plus kitchen stewards (cleaning, utensils) and a pastry/bakery team.

Smaller restaurants combine roles, but the discipline is the same.

steps.title: Dry-heat and moist-heat methods
steps.body:
- **Dry heat**: roasting, baking, grilling, tandoor, sautéing, shallow frying, deep frying — creates browning and crisp textures.
- **Moist heat**: boiling, simmering, steaming (idli, dhokla), poaching, braising/dum — tenderises tough cuts and keeps delicate foods moist.
- **Combination**: braising (brown first, then cook slowly in liquid).

Match the method to the ingredient: tender quick-cooking foods → dry heat; tough cuts → slow moist heat.

steps.title: Mise en place and knife basics
steps.body:
- Read the recipe fully, gather and prep all ingredients before cooking.
- Hold the knife firmly; curl the fingertips of your guiding hand (the 'claw') so knuckles guide the blade.
- A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one.
- Basic cuts: dice, julienne (thin strips), chiffonade (ribbons of leaves), mince.

steps.title: Kitchen safety
steps.body:
- Never leave hot oil unattended; dry wet food before frying to avoid splatter.
- For an oil fire, turn off the heat and cover the pan with a lid — **never pour water on burning oil**.
- Say 'behind you' and 'hot' when moving in a busy kitchen.
- Check gas connections; if you smell gas, don't switch anything on or off — open windows, close the regulator, leave and call for help.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Cook one vegetable two ways — e.g. potatoes boiled and potatoes roasted. Note how texture and taste change with moist versus dry heat.

activity.prompt: Dry heat or moist heat?

quiz.q: Who is second in command in a professional kitchen?
quiz.why: The sous chef is second in command in a professional kitchen, and runs the daily operations.

options: Everything prepared and in its place before cooking
quiz.why: Mise en place means having everything prepared and in its place before cooking starts. It makes service smooth.

quiz.q: A pan of oil catches fire. You…
options: Turn off heat and cover with a lid
quiz.why: For an oil fire, turn off the heat and cover the pan with a lid, which cuts off oxygen. Water would cause a dangerous flare-up.
Steaming cooks with moist heat (steam), so it is a moist-heat method. Grilling and frying are dry-heat or fat-based methods.

story.title: Why the bread was a brick

scenes.text: Ishita, 17, in Pune tried her first loaf using cups and spoons. It came out dense and flat.
Her aunt, a home baker, handed her a kitchen scale: 'Bakers weigh. Flour in a cup can vary a lot.'
They kneaded until the dough stretched thin without tearing, let it rise until doubled, and baked in a hot oven.
The loaf was tall and soft. Ishita now understands gluten, yeast and heat.

steps.title: Flour and gluten
steps.body:
Wheat flour contains proteins that form **gluten** when mixed with water and kneaded. Gluten makes a stretchy network that traps gas.

- **Bread** wants strong gluten: higher-protein flour, long kneading.
- **Cakes and biscuits** want tender crumb: less mixing once flour is added, often lower-protein flour (maida is commonly used).
- **Windowpane test**: stretch a small piece of bread dough thin — if light shows through without tearing, gluten is well developed.

steps.title: Leaveners: yeast, baking soda, baking powder
steps.body:
- **Yeast** is a living organism that eats sugars and produces **carbon dioxide** (and a little alcohol) — dough rises. It works best warm (not hot — very hot water kills it).
- **Baking soda** (sodium bicarbonate) needs an **acid** (curd, buttermilk, lemon, jaggery, cocoa) to release gas.
- **Baking powder** contains soda plus acid, so it needs only moisture and heat.
- Too much soda gives a soapy, bitter taste and brown colour.

steps.title: Baker's percentage — a worked example
steps.body:
Bakers express every ingredient as a percentage of **flour weight (flour = 100%)**.

A simple bread: flour 100%, water 62%, salt 2%, instant yeast 1%, sugar 3%, oil 4%.

For 500 g flour: water = 310 g, salt = 10 g, yeast = 5 g, sugar = 15 g, oil = 20 g.

Now you can scale to any batch size by changing only the flour weight.

steps.title: Ovens and eggless baking
steps.body:
- **Preheat** the oven fully; use an oven thermometer — many home ovens are off by several degrees.
- Typical ranges: cakes about **160–180 °C**, breads about **200–230 °C**; follow your recipe.
- Don't open the door early when baking cakes — they can sink.
- **Eggless baking** (popular in India) uses curd + baking soda, condensed milk, or other substitutes for structure and moisture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Measuring flour by cups and packing it; over-mixing cake batter (tough cake); expired yeast or baking powder; under-proofing or over-proofing dough; cutting bread while very hot (gummy crumb).

activity.prompt: Using baker's percentages, a recipe has water at 65%. How many grams of water do you need for 800 g of flour?

quiz.q: What gives bread its stretchy structure?
quiz.why: Gluten gives bread its stretchy structure. It traps the gas that makes dough rise.

quiz.q: Baking soda needs what to work?
quiz.why: Baking soda needs an acid, like curd or lemon, to react and release gas.

quiz.q: In baker's percentage, which ingredient is 100%?
quiz.why: In baker's percentage, flour is always 100%, and every other ingredient is a percentage of the flour's weight.

quiz.q: Why weigh rather than use cups?
options: Cup measures of flour vary a lot; weight is consistent
quiz.why: Cup measures of flour vary a lot, depending on how packed it is. Weighing is consistent, which matters in baking.

quiz.q: Very hot water added to yeast will…
quiz.why: Yeast is a living organism, and very hot water kills it. Then the dough won't rise.

lessons.title: Costing, pricing and starting a home food business

scenes.text: Sana in Lucknow baked cakes for friends and charged ₹400 for a 1 kg chocolate cake.
When she costed it — cocoa, butter, cream, gas, box, delivery — she was barely breaking even.
She calculated food cost, set a target, and registered with FSSAI before selling to the public.
Her prices rose to a fair level, and her FSSAI number on the box made new customers trust her.

steps.title: Recipe costing
steps.body:
1. List every ingredient with the amount used.
2. Find the cost per gram/ml from your purchase price (e.g. ₹480 per 1 kg butter = ₹0.48/g).
3. Multiply and add up — that's **ingredient (food) cost**.
4. Add packaging (box, board, label), gas/electricity, delivery.
5. Divide by portions if selling by piece.

steps.title: Worked example: food-cost percentage
steps.body:
Food cost % = ingredient cost ÷ selling price × 100.

Many restaurants aim for roughly **28–35%** food cost (depending on the business). Sana's cake ingredients cost ₹210. If she targets 35%:

Selling price = 210 ÷ 0.35 = **₹600**.

She then checks: does ₹600 cover packaging, gas, delivery and her time? If not, she adjusts the price or the recipe size.

steps.title: FSSAI registration and labelling
steps.body:
In India, food businesses need to be registered with or licensed by **FSSAI**:

- **Basic FSSAI registration** for small businesses (generally annual turnover up to ₹12 lakh), including many home bakers.
- **State licence** or **central licence** for larger turnovers or certain activities.

Packaged food labels should show the product name, ingredients, net quantity, date of manufacture/best before, FSSAI number, and the **green (veg) or brown (non-veg) symbol**, plus allergen information. Check the FSSAI portal for current rules.

steps.title: Growing a home food business
steps.body:
- Start with a small, excellent menu.
- Take advance payments for custom orders.
- Photograph your products well in natural light.
- Ask for reviews; handle complaints quickly and kindly.
- Keep simple accounts: sales, ingredient purchases, packaging, profit each month.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Cost one recipe you make well. Calculate the selling price at 30% and 35% food cost. Which feels right for your area and customers?

activity.label: Food-cost percentage of your menu item

bands.text: Very low food cost — high margin, but check quality and whether customers see value.
A common target range for many food businesses (about 28–35%). Make sure packaging, energy and time are covered too.
High — profit is thin once packaging, energy and labour are added. Consider pricing or portion changes.
Very high — you're likely losing money. Re-cost the recipe and reprice.

quiz.q: Ingredients cost ₹150 and you target 30% food cost. Selling price?
quiz.why: Food cost % = ingredient cost ÷ selling price. So price = 150 ÷ 0.30 = ₹500.

quiz.q: Which registration is typical for a small home bakery in India?
quiz.why: Small food businesses in India, like home bakeries, register with FSSAI. Basic FSSAI registration is typical for small ones.
Food cost % = ingredient cost ÷ selling price × 100.

quiz.q: Which should a packaged food label include?
options: Ingredients, date, FSSAI number, veg/non-veg symbol
quiz.why: A packaged food label should show ingredients, dates, the FSSAI number and the veg or non-veg symbol. This information protects consumers.

sources: FSSAI registration and labelling (general awareness)

questions.q: The temperature danger zone is roughly…
questions.why: The temperature danger zone is about 5–60 °C, where bacteria multiply fastest.
Steaming idli cooks with steam, so it's a moist-heat method.
Yeast ferments sugars and releases carbon dioxide gas. The gas gets trapped in the dough and makes it rise.
Raw meat should be stored below cooked food, and covered. That way its juices cannot drip onto food that is ready to eat.

courses.title: Appliances 1 · Fans and mixer-grinders
courses.summary: Diagnose and repair table/ceiling fans (capacitor-run induction motors) and mixer-grinders (universal motors with carbon brushes).
outcomes: Explain how a capacitor-run fan motor and a universal motor work

scenes.text: Anita's table fan hums but will not start until she spins it by hand.
That is a classic sign of a failed run capacitor.

steps.title: Fan motor
steps.body: Most household fans use a single-phase induction motor with a **run capacitor** (a few microfarads) that creates a phase shift so the motor starts and runs smoothly. A weak or open capacitor gives humming, slow speed or no start.

steps.title: Mixer motor
steps.body: Mixer-grinders use a **universal motor** (series-wound) with **carbon brushes** that wear down. Worn brushes cause sparking, weak power and burning smell.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: MAINS WARNING: 230 V AC can kill. Unplug the appliance, discharge any capacitors, and prove it is dead before touching internals. Never bypass thermostats, thermal fuses or earth. Never work alone. If you are not trained, do not open mains appliances - refer them to a qualified person.

steps.title: Height and electricity
steps.body: Use a stable ladder and a second person. Isolate at the MCB, not just the wall switch.

steps.title: Capacitance tolerance
steps.body: Use the exact value; a different value changes speed and heats the winding.

A heating element, thermostat or thermal fuse may be open.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: A resistive element (nichrome) converts electrical energy to heat. A bimetallic **thermostat** switches it off at the set temperature. A **thermal fuse** is a one-time safety device that opens at a fixed high temperature if the thermostat fails.

steps.title: Resistance from rating
steps.body: R = V squared / P. For 230 V and 1,000 W: R = 52,900 / 1,000 = 52.9 ohms. Current I = P / V = 1,000 / 230 = 4.35 A.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: MAINS WARNING: 230 V AC can kill. Unplug the appliance, discharge any capacitors, and prove it is dead before touching internals. Never bypass thermostats, thermal fuses or earth. Never work alone. If you are not trained, do not open mains appliances - refer them to a qualified person. Never bridge a thermal fuse.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: With the iron unplugged and switch/thermostat set on, measure resistance across the plug pins. Expect about the element resistance (for example around 50 ohms). OL means a break: test the cord, thermostat, thermal fuse and element separately.

steps.title: Divide and conquer
steps.body: Test each part by lifting one connection, or use the exposed terminals.

steps.title: Earth pin
steps.body: Check continuity from the earth pin to the metal soleplate: it should be near zero ohms.

steps.title: Core components
steps.body: **Resistor** limits current. **Capacitor** stores charge and smooths voltage. **Inductor** stores energy in a magnetic field. **Diode** lets current flow one way. **Transistor** switches or amplifies. **IC** packs many parts in one chip.

steps.title: Polarity matters
steps.body: Electrolytic capacitors, diodes, LEDs and ICs have a correct orientation. A reversed electrolytic can vent or burst.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: Work on low voltage first. MAINS WARNING: 230 V AC can kill. Never work on live equipment. steps.title: Example

scenes.text: Om connects an LED straight to a 9 V battery. It flashes and dies.

steps.title: The laws
steps.body: **V = I x R**, **P = V x I**. With R in ohms, I in amps, V in volts and P in watts. Combine: P = I squared x R = V squared / R.

steps.title: LED resistor

steps.title: Facts

courses.title: AC and home appliance basics
courses.summary: How air conditioners and fridges actually make cold, how to care for ACs, fridges, washing machines and geysers, how to read star labels, and how appliance technicians diagnose faults safely.
outcomes: Learners can explain the refrigeration cycle (compressor, condenser, expansion, evaporator)
Learners can explain tonnage, star ratings and why 24 °C saves energy
Learners can do safe user-level care for ACs, fridges, washing machines and geysers
Learners can follow a structured diagnosis and know which jobs need trained technicians

lessons.title: How cooling works

story.title: Why the outdoor unit is hot

scenes.text: In Nagpur's May heat, 12-year-old Tanvi touched the AC's outdoor unit and pulled her hand back. 'It's making cold — why is it hot?'
Technician Prakash smiled: 'The AC doesn't make cold. It carries heat out of your room and dumps it outside.'
He drew a loop: compressor → condenser → expansion valve → evaporator → back to compressor.
Tanvi's father, Sameer, realised why the outdoor unit must never be boxed in.

steps.title: The refrigeration cycle
steps.body:
A refrigerant circulates in a sealed loop:

1. **Compressor** squeezes refrigerant gas → it becomes hot, high-pressure gas.
2. **Condenser** (outdoor coil + fan) releases that heat outside → refrigerant turns into a high-pressure liquid.
3. **Expansion device** (capillary tube or expansion valve) drops the pressure suddenly → refrigerant becomes very cold.
4. **Evaporator** (indoor coil) absorbs heat from room air blown over it → refrigerant boils back into gas; room air becomes cooler and drier.

The same principle runs your fridge: the coil at the back or the warm sides are its condenser.

steps.title: Tons, BTU and star labels
steps.body:
- **1 ton of refrigeration = 12,000 BTU/hour ≈ 3.5 kW of cooling** — it describes heat removed, not weight.
- A rough guide many dealers use: about 1 ton for a small room (~100–120 sq ft), 1.5 ton for a medium room, 2 ton for larger rooms — but sun exposure, top floor, number of people and windows change this.
- The **BEE star label** shows energy efficiency; for ACs it uses **ISEER** (Indian Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio). More stars = less electricity for the same cooling. Star thresholds are revised periodically, so compare labels of the same year.
- **Inverter ACs** vary compressor speed instead of switching fully on/off — usually saving energy at part load.

steps.title: Why 24 °C
steps.body: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency recommends a default setting of about **24 °C**. Each degree higher saves energy (BEE has cited roughly 6% per degree). Combine with a ceiling fan — moving air makes 26 °C feel much cooler. Close curtains in the afternoon and seal door gaps.

steps.title: Refrigerants need trained hands
steps.body:
Refrigerants such as R-32, R-410A and R-290 are under pressure; some (R-32 mildly, R-290 highly) are **flammable**, and older R-22 is being phased out because it harms the ozone layer. Venting gas harms the environment. Gas charging, brazing and leak repair are for trained, equipped technicians.

A sealed system should not need regular 'gas top-ups' — **if gas is low, there is a leak** that must be found and fixed.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find the star label or rating plate on an AC or fridge at home. Note tonnage/capacity, star rating, refrigerant type and power input. Calculate units per month if used 6 hours a day.

Evaporator absorbs heat from room air

quiz.q: Where does an AC put the heat from your room?
quiz.why: An AC moves heat from the room to outside, through the condenser. It does not destroy heat.
One ton of refrigeration is a heat-removal rate of 12,000 BTU/h, which is about 3.5 kW. It describes cooling capacity, not weight.

quiz.why: A sealed AC system doesn't use up its gas. If it needs regular top-ups, there is a leak to find and fix.

quiz.q: BEE's recommended default AC temperature is about…
quiz.why: BEE recommends a default AC setting of 24 °C. It balances comfort and energy saving.

scenes.text: In Kolkata, water dripped from Dr. Roy's bedroom AC onto the bed.
Technician Shabnam switched off and unplugged, opened the front panel: filters thick with dust, the coil iced, the drain tray full.
She washed the filters, cleared the drain pipe and checked the slope of the pipe.
Cooling improved immediately. 'Most AC complaints are dirty filters and blocked drains,' she said.

steps.title: User-level care (anyone can do this)
steps.body:
- **Switch off and unplug / switch off the MCB** first.
- **Clean filters every 2 weeks** in heavy use: slide out, wash with plain water, dry in shade, refit.
- Keep the **outdoor unit** in the open with clear airflow; don't cover it while running; remove leaves and nests.
- Keep doors and windows closed while running.
- Book a **professional service** (coil cleaning, drain flushing, checks) before summer and as the manual suggests.

steps.title: Symptom → likely cause
steps.body:
- **Water dripping indoors** → blocked drain pipe, dirty filter causing ice, or poor drain slope.
- **Ice on indoor pipes** → dirty filter, low airflow or low refrigerant (leak).
- **Weak cooling** → dirty filters/coils, outdoor unit in hot enclosed space, wrong tonnage, low gas.
- **Outdoor fan runs, compressor doesn't** → often a failed capacitor, compressor protection, or supply issue (technician job).
- **Error code** on display → note it and check the manual; technicians use it to diagnose.

steps.title: Hidden dangers inside appliances
steps.body:
- **Capacitors** in AC outdoor units and motors can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged — trained technicians discharge them safely before touching.
- Outdoor units on high walls need **fall protection** — many technician injuries are falls.
- ACs usually need a dedicated **16 A circuit** with proper earthing; never run them from extension boards.

steps.title: Saving money on AC bills
steps.body: Set 24–26 °C with a fan, use sleep/eco mode, keep filters clean, shade the outdoor unit from direct afternoon sun without blocking airflow, and choose higher-star inverter models when buying. Units saved per year often pay back the extra cost of an efficient model within a few years.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With an adult, unplug an indoor unit and look at its filter. If it's dusty, wash it and note the date. Set a phone reminder every two weeks in summer.

quiz.q: How often should AC filters be cleaned in heavy use?
quiz.why: In heavy use, AC filters should be cleaned about every 2 weeks, as dust blocks airflow.

quiz.q: Why are AC capacitors dangerous even when unplugged?
options: They can store an electric charge
quiz.why: AC capacitors can store an electric charge even when unplugged. They can give a shock, so only trained people discharge them.
Washing filters is safe for users after switching off the AC. Gas charging, brazing and compressor work need a trained technician.

quiz.q: Indoor unit drips water. First thing to check?
quiz.why: When the indoor unit drips water, first check the drain pipe and filters. A blocked drain or a dirty filter is most common.

quiz.q: An AC should be powered from…
options: A dedicated properly earthed circuit (often 16 A)
quiz.why: An AC should run on a dedicated, properly earthed circuit, often 16 A. Extension boards and two-pin plugs are unsafe.

scenes.text: Technician Ravi in Bengaluru starts with a fridge 'not cooling': it's pushed tight against the wall with no air gap.
Next, a washing machine that won't drain — the drain filter is full of coins and hair.
Last, a geyser that hisses and drips from a small valve. 'That's the safety valve doing its job — the thermostat has failed.'
Ravi notes: two of three problems were user-fixable. He shows each customer what to check next time.

steps.title: Refrigerator
steps.body:
- Keep the fridge at about **3–5 °C** and freezer at about **−18 °C** for food safety.
- Leave a gap (as per manual, often a few cm) behind and at the sides for the condenser to release heat.
- Don't overfill — cold air must circulate.
- Check door gaskets: close the door on a paper strip; if it slides out easily, the seal leaks.
- Frost-free models defrost automatically; direct-cool models need manual defrosting when ice builds up.

steps.title: Washing machine
steps.body:
- Install **level** on a firm floor; unlevel machines vibrate and 'walk'.
- Clean the **drain/pump filter** (front-loaders, usually behind a small door at the bottom) and the lint filter regularly.
- Wipe the **door gasket** and leave the door open after use to stop mould.
- Use the right amount of detergent — too much causes residue and smells.
- Proper **earthing** is essential: a machine that tingles has a fault.

steps.title: Geyser (water heater)
steps.body:
- **Thermostat** controls temperature; the **safety / pressure-relief valve** releases pressure if it rises dangerously — it must never be blocked or plugged.
- In hard-water areas, scale builds up on the element; the **anode rod** (in many storage geysers) protects the tank and wears out over time.
- Geysers need a **16 A circuit, good earthing and an RCCB**. Many electricians also advise switching the geyser off before bathing.
- Signs to stop and call a technician: tingling from taps, scalding water, constant dripping from the valve, burning smell.

steps.title: Unplug first, always
steps.body: Before cleaning any appliance filter or gasket: switch off and unplug. Never open covers that need tools — motors, heaters, capacitors and wiring are inside. Never bypass a geyser's thermostat or safety valve.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do the paper-strip gasket test on your fridge door at three places. Check the gap behind the fridge. If you have a front-loader, find (don't open without an adult) the pump filter door.

statements.why: Never block it — it protects against tank rupture. Find the cause (often thermostat or pressure).

statements.s: Fridge food is safest at about 3–5 °C.
statements.why: Low temperatures slow bacterial growth.

statements.s: Using extra detergent always cleans better.
statements.why: Excess detergent leaves residue and smells.

quiz.why: Freezer temperature for food safety is about −18 °C.

quiz.q: A washing machine won't drain. A likely user-fixable cause?
quiz.why: A washing machine that won't drain is often blocked at the drain pump filter. Coins, hair and lint block it, and a user can often clear it.

options: Releases dangerous pressure and must never be blocked
quiz.why: A geyser's safety valve releases dangerous pressure, so it must never be blocked. This prevents the tank from rupturing.

quiz.q: A fridge door gasket check uses…
quiz.why: Close the fridge door on a paper strip. If the paper slides out easily, the seal is leaking.

quiz.q: Why install a washing machine level?
quiz.why: Installing a washing machine level prevents vibration and 'walking' during the spin. It also reduces wear.

scenes.text: Nasreen, 24, trained in refrigeration and AC repair in Lucknow and now runs her own service business.
A caller says, 'Fridge not cooling, change the compressor!' Another shop quoted ₹9,000.
Nasreen checks supply voltage, the condenser fan, thermostat and defrost system — the defrost heater had failed, so the evaporator was blocked with ice.
The repair costs a fraction of a compressor. The customer becomes her best referrer.

steps.title: A structured diagnosis
steps.body:
1. **Listen**: symptoms, when it started, sounds, smells, error codes, recent events (power cut, shifting).
2. **Check supply**: socket, plug, voltage, MCB/RCCB.
3. **Look and feel (safely)**: airflow, ice patterns, fan running, heat at condenser.
4. **Use the error code and service manual**.
5. **Test components** with the right meter (trained technicians only for live tests).
6. **Repair the root cause**, test fully, explain to the customer.

steps.title: Business basics
steps.body:
- Price clearly: visit charge + labour + parts; show old parts.
- Use genuine/quality parts; give a warranty on your work.
- Keep a service record per customer — remind them before summer (AC) or after a year (servicing).
- Use online listings carefully and maintain good reviews.
- Behave professionally inside homes: shoe covers, ID, explain before acting.

steps.title: Training
steps.body: Common routes: the ITI trade **Refrigeration and Air-Conditioning Technician**, short-term skilling courses, and manufacturer/brand service training. Refrigerant handling and brazing need hands-on supervised training with proper equipment; growing areas include inverter electronics, VRF systems in offices, and heat-pump water heaters.

steps.title: Refuse unsafe shortcuts
steps.body:
- Never bypass thermostats, overload protectors or safety valves.
- Never vent refrigerant deliberately.
- Never work at height without proper support; outdoor AC units on high walls need safe access.
- If you are not trained for a job, refer it — reputation lasts longer than one job's fee.

a.text: A customer insists: 'My AC isn't cooling. Just fill gas, it's been a year.' You find low pressure.

choices.label: Just top up the gas and leave
choices.feedback: The leak remains; cooling drops again and the customer pays twice.

choices.label: Explain that low gas means a leak; offer leak testing first

b.text: You find an oily spot at a flare joint on the indoor unit — a classic leak sign.

choices.label: Repair the joint, leak-test, then charge the correct amount
Tighten with extra force and hope
choices.feedback: Over-tightening can crack flares; without testing you don't know if it worked.

e1.text: Three weeks later the customer calls angrily. Topping up without fixing the leak wastes refrigerant and money.

e2.text: The AC cools well, the leak is gone, and you explained everything. The customer books annual servicing with you.

e3.text: The flare cracks; gas escapes again. Correct repair and leak testing are part of the job.

quiz.q: Customer demands a compressor change. You should first…
quiz.why: When a customer demands a compressor change, first diagnose systematically. Many 'compressor' complaints are caused by other faults.

quiz.q: An oily spot on an AC pipe joint often indicates…
quiz.why: Refrigerant carries oil, so a leak leaves an oily mark at a joint. An oily spot on an AC pipe joint often shows a refrigerant leak.

options: Showing old parts and a clear price breakdown
quiz.why: Showing old parts and giving a clear price breakdown builds trust. Transparency leads to repeat business.

quiz.q: Which ITI trade fits AC and fridge repair?
quiz.why: The ITI trade for AC and fridge repair is Refrigeration and Air-Conditioning Technician.

questions.q: Which part releases room heat outdoors?
questions.why: The condenser releases the room's heat outdoors. The evaporator absorbs heat inside.

questions.q: Most common user fix for weak AC cooling?
questions.why: Dirty filters are the most common cause of weak AC cooling, and a user can clean them.
1 ton of cooling is 12,000 BTU/h, which is about 3.5 kW.
More BEE stars means better energy efficiency, so lower running costs.

questions.q: A geyser safety valve drips constantly. You should…
options: Call a technician to check thermostat/pressure
questions.why: A geyser safety valve that drips constantly may mean a thermostat or pressure problem. Call a technician, and never plug or remove the valve.

questions.q: Why does an inverter AC often save energy?
options: It varies compressor speed rather than full on/off
questions.why: An inverter AC varies the compressor speed instead of switching fully on and off. This is efficient at part load.

questions.q: Ice on an indoor coil may be caused by…
questions.why: Ice on an indoor coil can be caused by a dirty filter (restricted airflow) or low refrigerant.

questions.q: A fridge has no gap behind it and runs constantly. Why?
questions.why: A fridge needs a gap behind it so the condenser can reject heat. With no gap, it can't, so it runs constantly.

questions.q: Why is R-290 handled with extra care?
options: It is a liquid at room temperature
questions.why: R-290 is propane, which is highly flammable. So it needs extra care when handling.

questions.q: A frost-free fridge's evaporator is blocked with ice and not cooling. Likely fault area?
questions.why: In a frost-free fridge, a failed defrost system (heater, timer or sensor) lets ice build up and choke airflow.

questions.q: Raising the AC setpoint from 22 °C to 25 °C saves roughly how much compressor energy using BEE's ~6% per °C estimate?
questions.why: Raising the setpoint by 3 °C saves about 3 × 6% ≈ 18% of compressor energy, using BEE's approximate figure.

questions.q: Why is regular 'gas top-up' a bad business practice?
options: It ignores the leak, harms the environment and repeats cost
questions.why: Regular gas top-ups ignore the leak. They also harm the environment and repeat the cost, so the leak should be fixed.

questions.q: Before touching an outdoor AC unit's terminals a trained technician must…
options: Isolate power and safely discharge capacitors
questions.why: Before touching terminals, a trained technician must isolate the power and safely discharge the capacitors, because they can store a charge.

courses.title: Two-wheeler and car maintenance
courses.summary: Understand how engines and EVs work, do the weekly checks that prevent breakdowns, care for a motorcycle or scooter, and handle warning lights, flat tyres and overheating safely.
outcomes: Learners can explain the four-stroke cycle and how EVs differ
Learners can do weekly checks: tyres, oil, coolant, brakes, lights
Learners can maintain a two-wheeler's chain, brakes and battery
Learners can respond correctly to warning lights, a flat tyre and overheating

scenes.text: Aman, 17, in Patna is saving for his first scooter. His uncle Rajesh runs a two-wheeler workshop.
Rajesh opens an old engine on the bench: piston, valves, spark plug. 'Four strokes,' he says. 'Mechanics remember them as suck, squeeze, bang, blow.'
Then he shows an electric scooter: battery, controller, hub motor — no oil change, no spark plug.
Aman decides to learn both. 'The future workshop needs both,' says Rajesh.

steps.title: The four-stroke petrol engine
steps.body:
1. **Intake**: piston moves down, intake valve opens, air–fuel mixture enters.
2. **Compression**: valves closed, piston moves up and squeezes the mixture.
3. **Power**: the **spark plug** fires; burning gas pushes the piston down — this is the work stroke.
4. **Exhaust**: piston moves up, exhaust valve opens, burnt gases leave.

The crankshaft turns the up-and-down motion into rotation → gearbox → wheels (via chain or belt in two-wheelers). **Diesel engines** have no spark plug: they compress air so much that injected fuel ignites from the heat (compression ignition).

steps.title: Electric vehicles
steps.body:
EVs use a **battery pack**, a **controller** and an **electric motor**. No engine oil, spark plugs or clutch; regenerative braking returns some energy to the battery. They still need **tyres, brakes, suspension, lights, coolant (in many cars for battery/motor cooling) and software updates**.

Safety: EV high-voltage systems (orange cables in cars) are only for trained technicians.

steps.title: Fluids and what they do
steps.body:
- **Engine oil**: lubricates, cools and cleans moving parts.
- **Coolant** (in liquid-cooled engines): carries heat to the radiator. Many small motorcycles and scooters are air-cooled.
- **Brake fluid** (hydraulic brakes): transmits lever/pedal force; absorbs moisture over time, so it is replaced at intervals.
- **Gear oil / transmission fluid**, **washer fluid**.

Use the grade specified in the **owner's manual** — the single most useful document for your vehicle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the wrong oil grade or 'any oil'.
- Ignoring service intervals in the manual.
- Overfilling oil above MAX (can damage seals).
- Continuing to drive after a red warning light comes on.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find your family vehicle's owner's manual (or the maker's website). Note the engine oil grade, service interval, tyre pressures (front/rear) and fuel type. Save them as a note on your phone.

activity.prompt: Order the four strokes of a petrol engine.
items: Power — spark ignites, piston pushed down

quiz.why: The power stroke, with the burning gas pushing the piston down, produces power. The others only prepare or clear the cylinder.

quiz.q: How does a diesel engine ignite fuel?
quiz.why: A diesel engine ignites fuel by compression heat. The air gets very hot when compressed, so no spark plug is needed.

quiz.q: Which does an EV NOT need?
quiz.why: An EV has no engine, so it doesn't need engine oil changes. It still needs brake, tyre and light checks.

quiz.q: The best source for your vehicle's oil grade and service interval is…
quiz.why: The owner's manual gives the correct oil grade and service interval for your exact vehicle. Specifications vary by model.

quiz.q: Brake fluid is replaced at intervals because…
quiz.why: Brake fluid absorbs moisture over time, which reduces braking performance. So it is replaced at set intervals.

scenes.text: Fatima drives from Pune to Mumbai every Friday. Her car felt heavy and used more fuel.
At a petrol pump, attendant Dinesh checked: front tyres were 22 psi; the door sticker said 33.
After correcting pressure, the steering felt light and her fuel efficiency improved.
Fatima now does a five-minute check every Sunday morning.

steps.title: Tyres
steps.body:
- Check pressure **when tyres are cold** (before driving far), using the figure on the **door-jamb sticker, fuel flap or owner's manual** — not the maximum printed on the tyre sidewall.
- Under-inflation → heavier steering, more fuel, overheating, blowouts. Over-inflation → less grip, harsh ride.
- Check **tread**: small raised bars in the grooves are **tread-wear indicators**; when the tread is level with them, replace the tyre.
- Look for cuts, bulges, nails. Don't forget the spare.

steps.title: Oil, coolant and fluids
steps.body:
- **Engine oil**: on level ground, engine off for a few minutes. Pull the dipstick, wipe, reinsert fully, pull again — level should be between MIN and MAX. Many scooters have a dipstick on the oil filler cap; some motorcycles have a sight glass.
- **Coolant**: check the reservoir level against marks **only when the engine is cold**. **Never open a hot radiator cap** — scalding coolant can spray out.
- **Brake fluid**: reservoir between marks; a sudden drop suggests a leak or worn pads.
- **Washer fluid**: top up with water and a suitable washer additive.

steps.title: Lights, horn, wipers, brakes
steps.body: Walk around with someone: headlights (low/high), indicators, brake lights, reverse light, hazard lights, horn, wipers. Test brakes gently at low speed before a journey. A brake pedal or lever that feels spongy or travels too far needs immediate checking.

steps.title: A memory aid
steps.body: Use the word **POWDER**: **P**etrol (fuel), **O**il, **W**ater (coolant, washer), **D**amage (body, tyres), **E**lectrics (lights, horn), **R**ubber (tyres, wiper blades).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do a POWDER check on a family vehicle with an adult. Record tyre pressures before and after correcting them.

activity.prompt: My weekly vehicle check (POWDER):
items: Engine oil between MIN and MAX (level ground, engine off a few minutes)
Coolant at the mark (cold engine only) and washer fluid topped up
Walked around for damage, nails, bulges
All lights, indicators, horn and wipers work
Tyre pressures correct when cold, including spare; tread above wear indicators

quiz.q: Where do you find the correct tyre pressure?
quiz.why: The correct tyre pressure is on the door-jamb sticker or in the manual. The sidewall number is the tyre's maximum.

quiz.q: When should you check tyre pressure?
quiz.why: Check tyre pressure when the tyres are cold. Heat from driving raises the pressure and the reading.

quiz.q: Why never open a hot radiator cap?
options: Pressurised hot coolant can spray and scald
quiz.why: Never open a hot radiator cap. The coolant is hot and under pressure, and it can spray and scald you.

quiz.q: Tread-wear indicators level with the tread mean…
quiz.why: When the tread-wear indicators are level with the tread, the tyre is worn to its limit and must be replaced.
In the POWDER check, R stands for Rubber: tyres and wipers.

scenes.text: Delivery rider Sandeep in Delhi rode 150 km a day and never oiled his chain.
One evening the rusty, loose chain jumped off the sprocket in traffic. He wasn't hurt, but lost a day's earnings.
Mechanic Salma showed him how to check slack, clean and lubricate the chain, and how worn sprockets look like shark teeth.
Sandeep now lubes his chain every weekend and his chain set lasts much longer.

steps.title: Chain and sprockets (motorcycles)
steps.body:
- **Slack**: with the bike on its stand and engine off, push the chain up and down at the midpoint of the lower run. Many motorcycles specify around **20–30 mm** of free play — **check your manual**.
- Too tight → strains bearings and the chain; too loose → can jump off.
- **Clean and lubricate** with chain lube regularly (commonly every few hundred km, and after rain or washing).
- Replace chain and sprockets together when sprocket teeth look hooked or the chain has tight spots.
- Scooters usually use a **CVT belt** inside a cover — replaced at service intervals.

steps.title: Brakes
steps.body:
- **Drum brakes**: check free play of the lever/pedal and adjust as per manual; many drums have a wear indicator.
- **Disc brakes**: check pad thickness through the caliper and brake fluid level.
- Many newer two-wheelers have **CBS** (combined braking) or **ABS**. Practise braking smoothly with both brakes.
- Squealing, grinding or a spongy lever → get it checked immediately.

steps.title: Battery, spark plug and air filter
steps.body:
- Keep battery terminals clean and tight; slow cranking or a weak horn suggests a weak battery.
- The spark plug and air filter are checked/cleaned/replaced at service intervals; a clogged air filter reduces mileage, especially in dusty conditions.
- Engine oil changes follow the manual's kilometre or time interval, whichever comes first.

steps.title: Safety while maintaining
steps.body: Engine and exhaust get very hot — let them cool. Keep fingers away from chain and sprocket; never check the chain with the engine running or the wheel turning under power. Petrol is highly flammable: no smoking, no flames.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With an adult, measure chain slack on a motorcycle at three points (roll the wheel by hand between checks, engine off). Note the tightest reading and compare with the manual.

activity.label: Measured chain free play (mid-point of lower run)

bands.text: Too tight — strains the chain, sprockets and gearbox bearings. Adjust as per manual.
On the tight side for many bikes — check your manual's range.
Within the range many motorcycles specify (often about 20–30 mm). Always confirm with your manual.
Too loose — the chain may slap or jump off. Adjust now and check for wear.

options: Engine off, at the midpoint of the lower run
quiz.why: Check chain slack with the engine off, at the midpoint of the lower run. That is a safe and accurate method.
Hooked, 'shark-tooth' sprockets are worn. Replace the chain and sprockets together, because worn sprockets quickly wear a new chain.
Most scooters transmit power through a CVT (continuously variable transmission) belt, not a chain.

options: Air or fluid problem — get it checked
quiz.why: A spongy disc-brake lever suggests air in the system or a fluid problem. Get it checked, since braking may be weak.

options: At the manual's km or time interval, whichever comes first
quiz.why: Change engine oil at the interval in the manual, by km or time, whichever comes first. Colour alone is not a reliable guide.

lessons.title: Warning lights, flat tyres and breakdowns

scenes.text: Rohan and his mother were driving from Ahmedabad to Udaipur at night when a red thermometer light came on.
Rohan pulled over safely, switched on hazard lights and turned off the engine. Steam rose from the bonnet.
He waited for the engine to cool rather than opening the radiator cap, then called roadside assistance.
A burst coolant hose was replaced. 'Stopping early saved the engine,' said the mechanic.

steps.title: Dashboard warning-light colours
steps.body:
- **Red** = serious, stop safely as soon as possible: oil pressure, engine temperature, brake system, battery/charging, airbag.
- **Amber/yellow** = check soon, drive carefully: check-engine light, ABS, tyre pressure (TPMS), low fuel.
- **Green/blue** = information: headlights, high beam, indicators, cruise control.

The owner's manual explains each symbol for your model.

steps.title: If the engine overheats
steps.body:
1. Turn off the AC; if safe, turn the heater to full to pull heat from the engine.
2. Pull over safely, hazard lights on, switch off the engine.
3. **Don't open the radiator cap** while hot.
4. Once fully cool, check coolant level and look for leaks.
5. Call roadside assistance if unsure. Driving on with an overheating engine can destroy it.

steps.title: Changing a flat tyre on a car — step by step
steps.body:
1. Stop on flat, firm ground well away from traffic; hazard lights on; handbrake on; passengers out to a safe place.
2. Place a warning triangle behind the car if you have one; wedge the diagonally opposite wheel.
3. **Loosen** wheel nuts slightly while the wheel is on the ground.
4. Place the jack at the **jacking point** shown in the manual; raise until the tyre clears the ground. Never put any body part under a car on a jack.
5. Remove nuts, swap wheel, hand-tighten nuts.
6. Lower the car; tighten nuts in a **criss-cross (star) pattern**.
7. Check spare pressure; re-check nut tightness after a short distance; get the flat repaired soon.

steps.title: Breakdowns and accidents
steps.body:
- Move to safety first; on highways stand away from traffic, behind barriers if possible.
- Call **112** for emergencies; most insurers and manufacturers offer roadside assistance — save the number in your phone.
- In India, the law protects **Good Samaritans** who help accident victims in good faith: they cannot be harassed or forced to give personal details.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With an adult, locate the jack, wheel spanner, spare and jacking points in your family car. Save the roadside assistance number in your phone.

a.text: You're driving at 60 km/h and the red oil-pressure light comes on.

choices.label: Keep going to your destination 30 km away
choices.feedback: Driving with no oil pressure can seize the engine in minutes.

choices.label: Slow down, signal, pull over safely and switch off

b.text: Stopped safely. The engine has been off for a few minutes. What now?

choices.label: Check the oil level with the dipstick on level ground
choices.feedback: Good — low oil is a common cause.

choices.label: Restart and rev to see if the light goes off
choices.feedback: Revving without oil pressure causes damage.

c.text: The dipstick shows oil far below MIN.

choices.label: Top up with the correct grade if available, check for leaks; if the light stays on, call for help
Pour in any liquid, even water
choices.feedback: Water or wrong fluids damage the engine.

e1.text: The engine seizes. A costly rebuild. Red lights mean stop safely as soon as possible.

e2.text: With oil topped up the light goes off; you drive gently to a workshop, which finds a leaking drain plug. Engine saved.

e3.text: Never put water or the wrong fluid in the engine. Call roadside assistance instead.

quiz.q: A red warning light generally means…
options: Stop safely as soon as possible
quiz.why: A red warning light generally means a serious fault. Stop safely as soon as possible.

quiz.q: When changing a wheel, you loosen nuts…
options: Slightly, while the wheel is still on the ground
quiz.why: Loosen the wheel nuts slightly while the wheel is still on the ground. The ground stops the wheel from turning.

quiz.q: Wheel nuts should be tightened in…
quiz.why: Tighten wheel nuts in a criss-cross (star) pattern. This seats the wheel evenly.

quiz.q: If the engine overheats you should NOT…
options: Open the radiator cap while hot
quiz.why: If the engine overheats, do not open the radiator cap while it is hot, because of the scalding risk. Pull over, turn off the AC and call for help.
112 is India's all-emergency number that connects to all emergency services. 101 is fire only and 1098 is Childline.

sources: Motor Vehicles Act (Good Samaritan provision) — general awareness

questions.q: Which stroke follows compression in a four-stroke engine?
questions.why: The four strokes go intake, compression, power, exhaust. So power follows compression.

questions.q: Check tyre pressure when tyres are…
questions.why: Check tyre pressure when the tyres are cold. Cold readings are accurate.
A red dashboard light means a serious fault: stop safely.
Engine oil lubricates moving parts, helps cool the engine and cleans it by carrying away dirt.

questions.q: Many motorcycles' chain free play is often in which range (check manual)?
questions.why: Many motorcycles have chain free play of about 20–30 mm, but the manual is the final word for your bike.

questions.q: Where should a car jack be placed?
options: At the jacking points shown in the manual
questions.why: Place a jack at the jacking points shown in the manual, which are reinforced. Other places can bend or damage the car.

options: Heavier steering, more fuel use, overheating
questions.why: Under-inflated tyres make steering heavier, use more fuel and overheat. This is dangerous.

questions.q: Why are EV orange cables only for trained technicians?
questions.why: The orange EV cables carry high voltage, which can be lethal. Only trained technicians should handle them.

questions.q: A sudden drop in brake fluid level suggests…
options: Leak or worn pads — check now
questions.why: A sudden drop in brake fluid suggests a leak or worn pads. Check it right away, because brakes are safety-critical.

questions.q: Temperature light comes on in traffic. Helpful immediate action?
options: Turn heater to full and AC off, then stop safely
questions.why: If the temperature light comes on, turn the heater to full and the AC off. The heater pulls heat from the engine and helps cool it. Then stop safely, and never open the radiator cap while hot.

questions.q: Why replace chain and sprockets together?
options: Worn sprockets quickly wear a new chain (and vice versa)
questions.why: A worn sprocket has hooked teeth that quickly wear out a new chain, and a worn chain damages new sprockets. So the chain and sprockets are replaced together as a set.

questions.q: The tyre sidewall says 'Max 44 psi'. The door sticker says 32 psi. Fill to…
questions.why: The sidewall number is the tyre's maximum pressure, not the recommendation. Fill to the vehicle's recommended pressure on the door sticker, 32 psi, measured when the tyres are cold.

questions.q: Oil far below MIN and red oil light. Best decision?
options: Drive to the workshop 30 km away
Top up correct grade if available, check for leaks; if the light stays, call assistance
questions.why: With oil far below MIN and a red oil light, run as little as possible to protect the engine. Top up with the correct grade if available, check for leaks, and call for help if the light stays on.

questions.q: Why should nobody put any body part under a car supported only by a jack?
questions.why: A jack can slip or fail, so no body part should go under a car held only by a jack. Use proper axle stands when working underneath.

courses.title: Driving theory: Indian road signs and rules
courses.summary: Learn India's three families of road signs, rules of the road, the learner's and driving licence process, the key traffic laws, and defensive driving — the knowledge tested for a learner's licence and needed for a lifetime of safe driving.
outcomes: Learners can identify mandatory, cautionary and informatory signs by shape and colour
Learners can apply keep-left, overtaking, right-of-way and roundabout rules
Learners can describe the learner's licence → driving licence process and required documents
Learners can state key laws on helmets, seat belts, drink-driving and mobile phones
Learners can practise defensive driving and respond to emergencies

lessons.title: The three families of road signs

scenes.text: Riya, 18, in Chandigarh books her learner's licence test online. Her brother laughs: 'Just guess, it's easy.'
She learns a trick from her driving instructor, Harpreet ji: 'Circles order you. Triangles warn you. Rectangles inform you.'
In the test, every unfamiliar sign suddenly makes sense from its shape and colour.
She passes — and her brother, who guessed, has to retake his.

steps.title: Mandatory (regulatory) signs — mostly circles
steps.body:
These are **orders**. Disobeying them is an offence.

- **Red circle** = prohibition: No entry (red circle with a white horizontal bar), No U-turn, No overtaking, No parking (blue circle with red border and a red diagonal), No stopping or standing (red cross on blue), Horn prohibited, Speed limit (number in a red circle), height/weight/width limits.
- **Blue circle** = compulsory action: Compulsory turn left, Compulsory keep left, Compulsory cycle track, Compulsory sound horn.
- Two special shapes: **STOP** is a red **octagon** — come to a complete stop. **GIVE WAY** is a red-bordered **inverted triangle** — slow down and give priority.

steps.title: Cautionary (warning) signs — red-bordered triangles pointing up
steps.body: These **warn** of hazards ahead so you can slow down and be ready: school ahead, pedestrian crossing, men at work, sharp bend left/right, hairpin bend, narrow road/bridge, speed breaker, slippery road, cattle, falling rocks, guarded/unguarded railway crossing, cross road, side road, roundabout ahead, steep ascent/descent, gap in median.

steps.title: Informatory signs — rectangles
steps.body: These **guide and inform**: hospital, first aid post, petrol pump, parking (white P on blue), eating place, light refreshment, rest house, destination and distance boards (often **green on national highways**, blue on other roads), park this side.

steps.title: Memory trick and road markings
steps.body:
**Circles command, triangles warn, rectangles inform.**

Road markings matter too: a **continuous (solid) centre line** — do not cross or overtake across it; **broken line** — you may cross when safe; **double solid** — never cross; **zebra crossing** — pedestrians have priority; **stop line** — stop behind it at signals.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: On your next trip, spot five signs and name their family and meaning. As a passenger, photograph any you don't recognise and look them up.

activity.prompt: Sort each sign into its family.

items.text: No entry — red circle with white bar

quiz.why: A red octagon is the STOP sign. You must stop completely at the line.
An inverted triangle with a red border is the Give Way sign. You must give way to traffic on the main road.
Blue circular signs give compulsory instructions, such as 'turn left' or 'keep left'. Red-bordered circles are prohibitions.
A solid centre line must not be crossed, so you must not overtake across it. Broken lines can be crossed when it is safe.
Upward-pointing red-bordered triangles are cautionary (warning) signs. They warn of hazards ahead.

sources: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 (as amended) — road signs, general awareness
Indian Roads Congress sign guidelines — general awareness

scenes.text: Kabir, a new driver in Bengaluru, freezes at a busy roundabout. Horns blare.
His instructor Deepa explains: 'Traffic already on the roundabout has priority. We go clockwise, keep left, and signal before we exit.'
At the next junction she shows him the stop line, the amber light, and why he must wait for pedestrians on the zebra crossing.
By the end of the week, Kabir drives through rush hour calmly.

steps.title: Keep left, overtake from the right
steps.body: India drives on the **left**. Keep to the left side of the road, letting faster vehicles pass on your right. **Overtake only from the right**, when the road ahead is clear and visible — never on bends, bridges, pedestrian crossings, near junctions or across a solid centre line. Do not speed up when someone is overtaking you.

steps.title: Right of way
steps.body:
- At an **uncontrolled junction of equal roads**, give way to traffic approaching from your **right**.
- Traffic on a **main road** has priority over traffic entering from a side road.
- At **roundabouts**, give way to traffic already on the roundabout; circulate **clockwise**.
- **Pedestrians** on zebra crossings have priority.
- **Ambulances, fire engines and police vehicles** on emergency duty: move aside and give way — obstructing them is an offence.

steps.title: Signals and lanes
steps.body:
- **Red**: stop behind the stop line. **Amber**: stop if you safely can; don't race it. **Green**: go if the junction is clear. **Flashing amber**: proceed with caution. **Flashing red**: stop, then proceed when safe.
- Use **indicators** well before turning or changing lanes; check mirrors and blind spot (**mirror–signal–manoeuvre**).
- On multi-lane roads, keep to your lane; use the right lane for overtaking, not cruising.
- Use **dipped headlights** in the city and when facing oncoming traffic; don't dazzle others with high beam.

steps.title: Common mistakes new drivers make
steps.body: Wrong-side driving to save a U-turn, overtaking from the left, stopping on zebra crossings, honking unnecessarily (and in silence zones near hospitals and schools), parking on footpaths, not signalling, and following too closely.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: As a passenger, count how many drivers signal before turning on a 10-minute stretch. Note three unsafe behaviours and the correct rule for each.

statements.s: In India you should normally overtake from the right.
statements.why: Vehicles keep left; overtaking is on the right.

statements.s: At a roundabout, vehicles entering have priority over those already circulating.
statements.why: Give way to traffic already on the roundabout.

statements.s: Roundabouts in India are driven clockwise.
statements.why: With left-hand traffic, circulation is clockwise.

statements.s: Amber means speed up to cross before red.
statements.why: Amber means stop if you can do so safely.

statements.s: You must give way to an ambulance with its siren on.
statements.why: Obstructing emergency vehicles is an offence.

quiz.q: At an uncontrolled junction of equal roads, give way to traffic from…
quiz.why: At an uncontrolled junction of equal roads, give way to traffic from your right. Check the rule for your local conditions too.

options: Highway with broken lines when clear
On bends, bridges, and near junctions/crossings
quiz.why: Never overtake on bends, bridges, or near junctions and crossings. Visibility is poor there, and many road users cross your path.
Mirror–signal–manoeuvre: check your mirrors, signal your intention, and then move. Observation comes first.
A flashing red signal is treated like a stop sign. Stop, and proceed only when it is safe.

quiz.q: Facing oncoming traffic at night you should use…
quiz.why: When facing oncoming traffic at night, use dipped beam so you don't dazzle other drivers. High beam can blind them.

lessons.title: Licences, documents and the law

scenes.text: Vishal and his friend Neha are stopped at a traffic checkpoint in Hyderabad.
Vishal shows his DL, RC, insurance and PUC on DigiLocker. Neha's pillion helmet is in her hand, not on her head.
The officer explains that pillion riders must wear helmets too, and issues a challan.
Neha buys her own ISI-marked helmet the same day.

steps.title: Learner's licence → driving licence
steps.body:
- **Age**: 16 for a gearless two-wheeler up to 50 cc (with parent/guardian consent); **18** for other motor vehicles such as cars and geared motorcycles.
- **Learner's licence (LL)**: apply through the official Parivahan Sarathi portal or RTO; there is a test on road signs and rules (many states offer it online). An LL is valid for **6 months**. While learning a car, display 'L' plates and drive only with a licensed driver beside you.
- **Driving licence (DL)**: you can take the driving test **after 30 days** from issue of the LL (and before it expires).
- Always check your state RTO's current procedure and fees.

steps.title: Documents you must carry
steps.body:
- **Driving licence**
- **Registration certificate (RC)**
- **Insurance** — at least **third-party insurance is compulsory**
- **PUC** (Pollution Under Control) certificate

Digital copies in **DigiLocker or mParivahan** are accepted as valid.

steps.title: Key laws (Motor Vehicles Act, as amended in 2019)
steps.body:
- **Helmets**: rider and pillion must wear a properly fastened, BIS-certified helmet (a limited exemption exists for Sikhs wearing a turban).
- **Seat belts**: for all occupants, front and rear.
- **Drink-driving**: the limit is **30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood**; penalties include heavy fines and imprisonment. The safest rule: if you drink, don't drive.
- **Mobile phones**: using a handheld phone while driving is an offence.
- **Juvenile driving**: if a minor commits a traffic offence, the guardian or vehicle owner can be held liable, the vehicle's registration can be cancelled, and the minor can be barred from getting a licence until a later age.
- Fines were raised sharply in 2019 and amounts can vary by state — check official state transport sites.

steps.title: Good Samaritan protection
steps.body: A person who helps an accident victim in good faith is protected from civil and criminal liability and cannot be forced to share personal details. Call **112**, give first aid if trained, and help get the victim to hospital — quick help in the first hour after a crash saves lives.

steps.title: Important note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Rules, fines and procedures change and vary by state — always check the official Parivahan portal and your state transport department.

cards.back: 6 months
30 days after the learner's licence is issued

cards.front: Minimum age for a car licence
cards.back: 18 years
30 mg alcohol per 100 ml blood (safest: zero)
Third-party insurance (at minimum)
DigiLocker or mParivahan
Rider AND pillion, BIS-certified, strap fastened

quiz.q: A learner's licence is valid for…
quiz.why: A learner's licence is valid for six months. After that it must be renewed.

quiz.q: Minimum age to drive a car on your own licence?
quiz.why: The minimum age to drive a car on your own licence is 18 years.
At least third-party insurance is compulsory. It covers harm to others, while comprehensive cover is optional.

quiz.q: Must a pillion rider wear a helmet?
quiz.why: Both the rider and the pillion rider must wear a helmet on a two-wheeler.

quiz.q: Which apps can hold valid digital vehicle documents?
quiz.why: DigiLocker and mParivahan are officially recognised platforms that can hold valid digital vehicle documents. Photos or WhatsApp copies are not.

sources: Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019 — general awareness
Parivahan Sewa (Ministry of Road Transport and Highways)

scenes.text: On a rainy evening on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway, Ananya kept a long gap behind a truck.
The truck braked suddenly for a stalled car. Ananya had time to slow smoothly; a tailgating car beside her swerved dangerously.
Her father, a bus driver for 25 years, had taught her: 'Expect the mistakes of others. Space is your safety.'
She arrives home safely and teaches her younger cousin the three-second rule.

steps.title: Keep a safe following distance
steps.body:
Pick a fixed object (a pole or sign). When the vehicle ahead passes it, count 'one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three'. If you reach the object before finishing, you're too close.

- **At least 3 seconds** in good conditions.
- **Double it** in rain, fog, at night or behind heavy vehicles.
- Braking distance grows roughly with the **square of speed**: double the speed ≈ four times the braking distance.

steps.title: See, predict, act
steps.body:
- **Look far ahead**, not just at the vehicle in front.
- **Check mirrors** every few seconds and before braking or turning.
- Watch for **vulnerable road users**: pedestrians, cyclists, children, animals.
- **Blind spots**: big vehicles can't see you beside or close behind them — if you can't see the driver's mirrors, they can't see you.
- Never drive tired: take breaks about every two hours on long drives.

steps.title: Rain, fog and night
steps.body:
- Slow down; use dipped headlights (and fog lamps if fitted) in fog, not high beam.
- Avoid sudden braking or steering on wet roads; on waterlogged roads, if you can't see the road surface, don't enter.
- If the vehicle skids, ease off the accelerator and steer gently where you want to go.

steps.title: At an accident scene
steps.body:
1. Park safely ahead, hazards on.
2. Protect the scene; watch traffic.
3. Call **112** with the exact location (landmarks, km stone).
4. Don't move injured people unless there's immediate danger (fire, traffic) — spinal injury risk.
5. If trained, give first aid: check breathing, control bleeding with firm pressure.
6. Stay calm; you're protected as a Good Samaritan.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: As a passenger, practise the three-second count on a highway. How often do drivers keep enough distance?

a.text: It's raining heavily at night. The car ahead is close and you're running late.

choices.label: Overtake quickly from the left to get past
choices.feedback: Overtaking from the left, in rain, is illegal and dangerous.

choices.label: Slow down and increase the gap to about 6 seconds
choices.feedback: Correct — space and time are safety.

b.text: Your phone rings. It's your manager.

choices.label: Pick it up — just a quick call
choices.feedback: Handheld phone use is illegal and distracts you at the worst time.

choices.label: Let it ring; call back after stopping safely

c.text: Ahead, a scooter rider has fallen. Traffic is slowing.

choices.label: Drive past — someone else will help
choices.feedback: Every minute matters, and you're protected by the Good Samaritan law.

choices.label: Stop safely ahead, hazards on, call 112 with location, help without moving them unnecessarily

e1.text: A bus pulls into your path; you narrowly avoid a crash. Patience is part of driving skill.

e2.text: You miss the brake lights ahead and brake hard. Next time, let it ring.

e3.text: The rider waits a long time for help. Helping is protected and lifesaving.

e4.text: Help arrives quickly. You drove safely, stayed focused and may have saved a life.

quiz.q: The minimum safe following gap in good conditions is about…
quiz.why: Keep a following gap of at least 3 seconds in good conditions, and more in bad conditions. One car length is far too little at speed.

quiz.q: Doubling speed increases braking distance by about…
quiz.why: Braking distance grows roughly with the square of speed. Doubling the speed makes it about 4 times longer.

quiz.q: If you can't see a truck driver's mirrors…
quiz.why: If you can't see a truck driver's mirrors, the driver can't see you either. You are in the blind spot.
In fog use dipped beam or fog lamps. High beam reflects off the fog and makes visibility worse.

quiz.q: At an accident, you generally should NOT…
options: Move the injured unless in immediate danger
quiz.why: Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger, because moving can worsen spinal injuries. Call 112, warn traffic and use hazard lights.

questions.q: A sign with a red circle generally means…
questions.why: A sign with a red circle generally prohibits something, such as no entry or no parking.
India drives on the left. Keep left, and overtake on the right.

questions.q: Which document is NOT required to be carried?
questions.why: You need to carry your DL, RC, insurance and PUC. A school certificate is not needed while driving.

questions.q: A green highway destination board is…
questions.why: A green highway destination board is an informatory sign. Guide signs give directions and distances.

questions.q: You may appear for the DL test after getting an LL in…
questions.why: You can appear for the driving licence test after holding a learner's licence for 30 days.

options: From the right when clear and visible
questions.why: Overtake from the right, when the road ahead is clear and visible. Never on bridges or bends.

questions.q: The drink-driving limit in India is…
questions.why: The drink-driving limit in India is 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood.

questions.q: At a roundabout you give way to…
questions.why: At a roundabout, give way to traffic already on the roundabout. Circulating traffic has priority.

questions.q: A blue circle with a red border and a red diagonal is…
questions.why: A blue circle with a red border and a red diagonal is the No Parking sign. A compulsory sign would have no red border.

questions.q: Doubling speed from 40 to 80 km/h changes braking distance roughly to…
questions.why: Braking distance depends roughly on the square of speed. Doubling from 40 to 80 km/h makes it about four times longer.

questions.q: A minor drives and commits an offence. Under the 2019 amendment…
options: The guardian/owner can be held liable and registration cancelled
questions.why: Under the 2019 amendment, if a minor commits an offence while driving, the guardian or owner can be held liable and the vehicle's registration can be cancelled.

questions.q: In heavy rain the following gap should be…
questions.why: In heavy rain, roads are slippery and braking takes longer. So keep about double the usual following gap.

questions.q: A Good Samaritan who helps an accident victim…
options: Is protected from harassment and liability when acting in good faith
questions.why: A Good Samaritan who helps an accident victim in good faith is protected from harassment and liability by law. They don't have to give personal details or pay hospital fees.

questions.q: Which correctly lists the three sign families by shape?
options: Circles order, triangles warn, rectangles inform
Circles warn, triangles order, rectangles inform
questions.why: Circles give orders (mandatory or prohibitory), triangles warn, and rectangles give information.

trades-home-technical.title: Hunar: Home trades — electrical, plumbing, carpentry
trades-home-technical.description: Hands-on home trades — electrical safety, plumbing and carpentry — explained so you can work safely, serve customers well and earn. Continued in 'Hunar: Appliances, vehicles & driving'.

courses.title: Electrician basics — safety first
courses.summary: Understand how electricity reaches and moves through an Indian home, how MCBs, RCCBs and earthing protect you, what the wire colours mean, and the safe-isolation routine every electrician follows before touching anything.
outcomes: Learners can explain volts, amps, watts and units (kWh) with home examples
Learners can describe and follow the safe-isolation routine: switch off, lock and tag, test dead
Learners can tell what an MCB, an RCCB and earthing each protect against
Learners can identify Indian wiring colours and socket ratings, and know never to trust colour alone
Learners can respond correctly to an electric-shock emergency

lessons.title: How electricity works in your home

story.title: Arjun's first day at the workshop

scenes.text: Arjun, 19, joins Rafiq bhai's electrical shop in Indore as a helper. On day one Rafiq bhai hands him a tester and says: 'First you understand. Then you touch.'
They visit a flat where the geyser keeps tripping the switch. The owner asks, 'Why can't you just put a bigger fuse?'
Rafiq bhai does a quick sum on a scrap of paper: watts ÷ volts = amps. 'The wire decides the fuse. Not the customer,' he says.
Arjun realises electricity is not magic — it is numbers, and the numbers keep people alive.

steps.title: Voltage, current and power — in plain words
steps.body:
Think of electricity like water in a pipe.

- **Voltage (V)** is the push, like water pressure. Indian homes get about **230 V single-phase AC at 50 Hz**. Bigger buildings and some homes take **three-phase supply (about 400–415 V between phases)**.
- **Current (A, amperes)** is how much electricity flows, like litres per second.
- **Power (W, watts)** is how fast energy is used. **Power = Voltage × Current** (P = V × I).
- **Resistance (Ω, ohms)** opposes flow. Ohm's law: **V = I × R**.

A 230 V supply is enough to stop a human heart. A current of only tens of milliamps through the chest can be fatal. That is why every step in this course starts with safety.

steps.title: Worked example: how many amps does a geyser draw?
steps.body:
A geyser is rated **2000 W**. Supply is **230 V**.

I = P ÷ V = 2000 ÷ 230 ≈ **8.7 A**.

So it must go on a circuit and socket rated well above 8.7 A — in India that means a **16 A socket** on a suitably sized wire and breaker, not a small 6 A socket.

Now you try: a 1000 W iron → 1000 ÷ 230 ≈ 4.3 A. A 60 W fan → about 0.26 A.

steps.title: What is a 'unit' on your electricity bill?
steps.body:
One **unit = 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh)** = using 1000 W for 1 hour.

- 2000 W geyser for 30 minutes = 2 kW × 0.5 h = **1 unit**
- 10 LED bulbs of 9 W for 5 hours = 90 W × 5 h = 450 Wh = **0.45 unit**
- A 1.5-ton AC can draw roughly 1.2–1.8 kW depending on model and star rating — so a few hours a day adds many units.

Multiplying units by your tariff (₹ per unit, set by your state's electricity regulator) gives the energy charge.

steps.title: Phase, neutral and earth
steps.body:
A home circuit has three conductors:

- **Phase (live / line)**: carries the 230 V. This is the dangerous one.
- **Neutral**: the return path. It is close to earth potential *in normal conditions*, but it can carry current and can become dangerous if there is a fault — never treat neutral as safe.
- **Earth**: a safety path to the ground (via an earth pit or the supply earth). It normally carries no current; it carries fault current so that protection devices trip.

Switches must always break the **phase**, never only the neutral. A switch on the neutral leaves the bulb holder live even when 'off'.

steps.title: Common mistakes beginners make
steps.body:
- 'It's only 230 volts' — 230 V kills people every year in India.
- 'The switch is off so it's safe' — the switch might be on the neutral, or the circuit may be fed from elsewhere.
- Replacing a tripping breaker with a bigger one — the breaker protects the **wire**; upsizing it lets the wire overheat and start a fire.
- Wet hands, bare feet, metal ladders — each one lowers your body's resistance.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Look at the rating sticker on three appliances at home (fan, fridge, mixer). Write the watts. Calculate the amps (W ÷ 230) and the units used per day for your family's typical use. Compare with your bill.

activity.prompt: A 1500 W induction cooktop runs on 230 V. About how many amperes does it draw? (Round to 1 decimal)

quiz.q: What is the normal single-phase supply voltage in Indian homes?
quiz.why: India's standard single-phase household supply is about 230 V AC at 50 Hz. 110 V and 12 V are not the normal home supply.

quiz.q: A 2000 W appliance used for 2 hours consumes how many units?
quiz.why: Units are kWh. 2000 W is 2 kW, and 2 kW × 2 h = 4 kWh, or 4 units.

quiz.q: Which conductor should a light switch break?
quiz.why: Switching the phase makes the fitting dead when off. Switching only neutral leaves it live.

quiz.q: Why should you never fit a bigger breaker because one keeps tripping?
options: The breaker protects the wire; a bigger one lets the wire overheat
It is illegal to buy one
quiz.why: A breaker is sized to protect the wire. A bigger one would not trip when the wire overheats, which risks fire. A tripping breaker is a warning to find the fault.
Power in watts = voltage × current: P = V × I.

sources: Ohm's law (standard physics)
Central Electricity Authority safety regulations — general awareness

lessons.title: Never work live: the safe-isolation routine

scenes.text: In Lucknow, Sunil was changing a switch board. He touched it with his neon tester screwdriver — no glow. He started unscrewing.
A spark jumped. Sunil was lucky: a small burn and a bad fright. The board was fed from a second circuit, and his tester's bulb was weak.
His instructor, Kavita ma'am, made the whole batch learn one routine: isolate, lock, tag, prove, test, prove.
'A tester that shows nothing has not proved anything,' she said. 'You must prove the tester works before and after.'

steps.title: Rule one: never work on live circuits
steps.body:
Electricity can kill. This course teaches understanding and safe habits; it does not make you a licensed electrician. Work on building wiring should be done by, or under the supervision of, a licensed electrician as required by your state's electrical licensing rules.

Professional electricians assume **every wire is live until they have proved it dead** with a proper tester. Live working is a specialist activity done only by trained, authorised people with insulated tools and PPE — it is not something a learner, helper or homeowner does.

steps.title: The safe-isolation routine (learn it in order)
steps.body:
1. **Identify** the circuit you will work on (check the labelled distribution board).
2. **Switch off** the correct MCB — or the main switch if unsure.
3. **Lock and tag**: lock the breaker off if a lock-off device is available, and hang a tag: 'Do not switch on — work in progress — name, phone'. Tell everyone in the house.
4. **Prove your tester** on a known live source (a socket you know is on).
5. **Test dead**: test between phase–neutral, phase–earth and neutral–earth at the point of work.
6. **Prove your tester again** on the known live source — this confirms it did not fail during the test.
7. Only now start work. If anything is unclear, stop and ask.

steps.title: Why the neon tester screwdriver is not enough
steps.body: The cheap neon screwdriver tester is useful for a quick hint, but it is **not proof**: it depends on your body as part of the path, may not glow in bright light, can fail silently, and does not test between phase and neutral. Use a **two-pole voltage tester or a multimeter in the correct AC voltage range** for proving dead, and still follow the prove–test–prove routine.

steps.title: Basic PPE and habits
steps.body:
- Dry hands, dry floor; rubber-soled shoes.
- Insulated tools in good condition (no cracked handles).
- Wooden or fibreglass ladder — never aluminium near wiring.
- Remove rings, watches and metal chains.
- One-hand rule while testing where possible, to avoid current across the chest.
- Never work alone on anything bigger than a simple fitting.

steps.title: If someone gets an electric shock
steps.body:
1. **Do not touch them** while they may still be in contact with the supply.
2. **Switch off** at the MCB / main switch or pull the plug.
3. If you cannot switch off, push the source away with a **dry non-conducting object** (dry wood, plastic) while standing on something dry.
4. Call **112**.
5. If they are not breathing normally, start **CPR** and continue until help arrives. Cool burns with cool running water.
6. Anyone who has had a significant shock should be checked by a doctor — heart rhythm problems can appear later.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Without opening anything, walk to your home's distribution board. Find the main switch and the MCBs. Are they labelled? Write a simple label list (e.g. 'MCB 3 — kitchen sockets') with an adult or the house owner.

activity.prompt: Put the safe-isolation routine in the correct order.
items: Identify the circuit on the distribution board
Lock off and tag the breaker
Prove the tester on a known live source
Test the circuit dead at the point of work
Prove the tester again on the known live source

quiz.q: Your tester shows no voltage on a circuit. What must you do before trusting it?
options: Prove the tester on a known live source before and after
Switch the MCB on and off quickly
