quiz.why: A tester that has failed also shows no voltage. So prove it on a known live source before and after testing. This is prove–test–prove.

quiz.q: Why hang a tag on the switched-off breaker?
options: It is needed for the bill
So no one switches it on while you work
quiz.why: A tag (and lock) on the switched-off breaker stops someone from switching it back on while you are working.

quiz.q: Someone is stuck to a live wire. First action?
options: Wait for them to let go
Switch off the supply or push the source away with dry wood
quiz.why: Never touch them directly; cut the supply or separate them using a dry non-conductor.

quiz.q: Which ladder is safest near electrical work?
quiz.why: Wooden or fibreglass ladders do not conduct electricity, so they reduce the risk of a current path through you. Steel and aluminium conduct.

quiz.q: Which number should you call in India for an emergency?
quiz.why: 112 is India's all-emergency number. 1098 is Childline and 14416 is Tele-MANAS.

sources: Electrical safe-isolation practice (industry standard)
Basic first aid for electric shock

lessons.title: Your distribution board: MCB, RCCB and earthing

scenes.text: In Kochi, Mrs. Thomas's power went off every time it rained. She called electrician Biju.
Biju opened only the outer cover of the board and pointed: 'This is your RCCB. It tripped because current is leaking somewhere — probably water in the outdoor light.'
He isolated the circuit, found water inside the garden lamp, dried it, replaced the gasket and fitted a weatherproof fitting.
'Never remove the RCCB because it trips,' he told her. 'It just told you about a leak that could have killed someone.'

steps.title: What lives in a distribution board (DB)
steps.body:
From the meter, supply goes to your **DB**. Typically you will see:

- A **main switch / isolator** (switches off everything).
- An **RCCB** (or several) — protects people against leakage/earth-fault current.
- Several **MCBs**, one per circuit (lights, sockets, AC, geyser, kitchen).
- **Neutral and earth bars** behind the cover.

Only the switch handles and test button are meant for the user. Opening the inner cover exposes live parts — that is a job for a licensed electrician.

steps.title: MCB — protects the wire
steps.body:
A **Miniature Circuit Breaker** trips on:

- **Overload** — too much current for too long (e.g. three heaters on one circuit). A heat-sensitive (thermal) part trips it.
- **Short circuit** — phase touching neutral/earth, huge current instantly. A magnetic part trips it in a fraction of a second.

Common ratings: 6 A, 10 A, 16 A, 20 A, 32 A. 'B' curve MCBs are common for homes; 'C' curve tolerate higher starting currents (motors, ACs). The rating is chosen to match the **wire size**, so the wire never overheats.

**An MCB does not protect you from electric shock** — a shock current of a few tens of milliamps is far too small to trip a 16 A breaker.

steps.title: RCCB — protects people
steps.body:
A **Residual Current Circuit Breaker** compares the current going out on phase with the current returning on neutral. If they differ — meaning some current is leaking to earth, perhaps through a person — it trips.

- **30 mA** RCCBs are used for protection of people.
- 100 mA / 300 mA types are used mainly for fire protection.
- An RCCB alone does **not** protect against overload or short circuit — it is used together with MCBs (or as an **RCBO**, which combines both).
- Press the **'T' test button** regularly (e.g. monthly) — it should trip. If it does not, call an electrician.

steps.title: Earthing
steps.body:
The earth wire connects metal bodies of appliances (geyser, fridge, washing machine, iron) to the ground. If a live wire touches the metal body, fault current flows to earth and the MCB/RCCB trips, instead of the metal staying live waiting for someone to touch it.

Bad signs: tingling from a washing machine, sparks from a tap, a metal body that 'bites'. These mean an earth or insulation fault — stop using the appliance and call an electrician. Earth pits need periodic checking, especially in dry areas.

steps.title: Dangerous 'fixes' you must refuse
steps.body:
- Bypassing or removing an RCCB because it 'trips too much'.
- Wrapping wire around a fuse or using a thicker fuse wire.
- Using a two-pin plug for an appliance that needs earth.
- Joining earth to neutral to stop tripping.

Each of these turns a safety device off and leaves a hidden killer behind.

steps.title: Worked example: which device tripped and why?
steps.body:
- **Geyser circuit MCB (16 A) trips after 10 minutes, wire warm** → overload or loose connection heating up. Check load and connections (licensed electrician).
- **MCB trips instantly with a bang when you switch on a fan** → short circuit in the fan or wiring.
- **RCCB trips when washing machine runs, MCB fine** → leakage to earth in the machine (e.g. heater element or wet wiring).

Reading which device tripped is the first diagnostic clue.

activity.prompt: Which device mainly protects against each problem?

items.text: Too many heaters on one circuit
Current leaking through a person to earth
Wet outdoor lamp leaking to earth
Faulty washing machine body becoming live

quiz.q: What trip current is typical for an RCCB that protects people?
quiz.why: A 30 mA RCCB is used for personal protection, since it trips at a leakage current small enough to prevent serious shock.

quiz.q: Does a 16 A MCB protect you from electric shock?
options: No — shock currents are far too small to trip it
quiz.why: Shock currents of tens of milliamps cannot trip a 16 A MCB; that is the RCCB's job.

quiz.q: The RCCB test button should be pressed…
options: Regularly, e.g. monthly — it should trip
quiz.why: Press the RCCB test button regularly, such as monthly. It should trip, which shows the mechanism works.

quiz.q: A washing machine gives a mild tingle. What does it suggest?
options: Earth or insulation fault — stop using it
quiz.why: A tingle from a washing machine's metal body points to an earth or insulation fault. Stop using it, unplug it and get it repaired.

options: A device combining RCCB and MCB functions
quiz.why: An RCBO combines the functions of an RCCB (leakage protection) and an MCB (overcurrent protection) in one device.

sources: IS/IEC standards for MCBs and RCCBs (general awareness)
Manufacturer guidance on RCCB test button

lessons.title: Wires, colours and sockets in India

scenes.text: Priya, an electrical diploma student in Pune, visits two buildings. In the old one, phase is red, neutral black, earth green.
In the new flat, she sees brown, blue and green-yellow, like on imported appliances.
'Which one is correct?' she asks her mentor, Mr. Deshpande.
'You will meet both,' he says. 'Learn both — and then test, because someone may have used any colour they had.'

steps.title: Wiring colours you will meet in India
steps.body:
**Traditional Indian practice** (very common in existing buildings):

- Phase: **red** (in three-phase: **red, yellow, blue** for the three phases)
- Neutral: **black**
- Earth: **green** (or green with yellow stripe)

**International (harmonised) colours**, seen on most appliance cords and in many newer installations:

- Live/phase: **brown** (three-phase: brown, black, grey)
- Neutral: **blue**
- Earth: **green-and-yellow**

Notice the trap: **black is neutral in the old scheme but can be a phase in the new three-phase scheme**. Colours are a guide, never proof. **Always test.**

steps.title: Wire sizes (copper) — common practice
steps.body:
Wire size is the cross-section area in square millimetres (sq mm). Common practice in Indian homes:

- **1.0–1.5 sq mm**: lighting and fan points
- **2.5 sq mm**: 6 A socket circuits
- **4 sq mm**: 16 A power sockets — geyser, AC, oven (larger ACs or long runs may need more)
- **6 sq mm and above**: main incoming lines, depending on load

Exact sizes depend on length, load, how many wires share a conduit, and the applicable standards — a licensed electrician calculates them. Use ISI-marked wire from reputable makers; fake 'lightweight' wire with less copper is a known fire risk.

steps.title: Sockets and plugs
steps.body:
Indian homes mainly use round-pin three-pin sockets:

- **6 A sockets (smaller)** — phone chargers, TVs, laptops, fans, lamps.
- **16 A sockets (larger)** — geysers, ACs, room heaters, microwave ovens, washing machines.

The top (thicker) pin is **earth**. Use the right size plug; never force a 16 A appliance into a 6 A socket with an adapter, and never run heaters from extension boards or multi-plug adapters. Modular switches with shutters are safer for homes with children.

steps.title: Mistakes that start fires
steps.body:
- Twisting wires together and wrapping with tape instead of using proper connectors/terminals.
- Overloaded extension boards ('octopus' sockets).
- Loose terminal screws — they arc and heat up; look for brown/black marks.
- Thin wire feeding a heavy load.
- Using any colour wire 'because that's what was in the bag'.

steps.title: Try this (no tools needed)
steps.body: Look at the plug of a geyser or AC and a phone charger at home. Which socket size does each use? Look at an appliance cord where the outer sheath is cut back at the plug: can you see brown, blue and green-yellow? Note anything with burn marks or a warm plug — tell an adult.

activity.prompt: Match each wire or item with its meaning.

quiz.q: In the harmonised scheme, blue is…
quiz.why: In the harmonised scheme, brown is live (phase), blue is neutral, and green-yellow is earth.

quiz.q: In traditional Indian wiring, earth is usually…
quiz.why: In traditional Indian wiring, earth was usually green. Green-yellow is now common.

quiz.q: Why can't you rely on colours alone?
options: Different schemes and past mistakes mean a wire may not be what its colour suggests
quiz.why: You can't rely on colour alone, because old and new colour schemes mix and installers make mistakes. So a wire may not be what its colour suggests. Always test.

quiz.q: Which socket suits a 2 kW geyser?
quiz.why: A 2 kW geyser draws about 2000 ÷ 230 ≈ 8.7 A. That needs a 16 A socket on a suitable circuit, not a 6 A socket or an extension board.

quiz.q: Which pin is earth in an Indian three-pin plug?
quiz.why: In an Indian three-pin plug, the larger, thicker top pin is the earth pin.

sources: IS 732 (code of practice for electrical wiring installations) — general awareness
IEC 60445 (identification of conductors)

lessons.title: Simple jobs, fault-finding and your career path

scenes.text: Meena, 22, has finished her ITI Electrician course in Jaipur and works with a contractor. Her first solo call: 'Fan not working, regulator hot.'
She switches off the MCB, tags it, proves her tester, tests dead — and only then opens the switchboard.
A loose, blackened terminal on the regulator. She replaces the regulator, tightens terminals properly and restores power.
She explains to the customer what happened and why loose connections are dangerous. The customer books her again for the whole flat.

steps.title: A fault-finding mindset
steps.body:
Professionals diagnose before they replace.

1. **Ask**: what happened, when, any smell, sound, or trip?
2. **Look** (with power off): burn marks, melted plastic, loose wires.
3. **Check the simple things first**: is the MCB on? Is the bulb fine? Is the regulator working?
4. **Isolate and test** using the safe-isolation routine.
5. **Fix the cause**, not just the symptom (e.g. replace a burnt terminal, don't just change the bulb).
6. **Test after repair** and explain to the customer.

steps.title: Worked example: replacing a bulb holder (supervised practice)
steps.body:
Under supervision, after isolation and testing dead:

- Note which wire goes where (take a photo).
- Loosen terminal screws, remove old holder.
- Strip insulation only as much as the terminal needs — no bare copper outside the terminal.
- Phase to the centre contact (for an Edison screw holder), neutral to the outer shell.
- Tighten firmly, tug-test each wire, refit cover.
- Restore power, test, remove your tag.

If any wire is brittle, burnt or the box is damaged — stop and report it.

steps.title: Training and licensing paths
steps.body:
- **ITI Electrician** trade (two years) is a common route; there are also short-term skill courses under national skilling schemes.
- Polytechnic **Diploma in Electrical Engineering** and B.Tech/BE go further into design.
- To do wiring work, electricians obtain a **wireman/electrician permit or supervisor certificate** and contractors a **contractor licence** from the state electrical licensing authority. Requirements differ by state — check your state's licensing board.
- Careers: house wiring, industrial maintenance, solar PV installation, panel wiring, lift and HVAC electrical, facility management.

steps.title: Professional habits customers remember
steps.body:
- Arrive on time, wear clean clothes, carry shoe covers.
- Give a clear estimate before starting; explain extra charges before doing extra work.
- Never leave exposed wires, and clean up.
- Refuse unsafe requests politely (bypassing an RCCB, oversizing a breaker) and explain why.
- Keep a simple job record: date, address, work done, materials, payment.

steps.title: Know when to say no
steps.body:
As a learner or helper, do not attempt: work inside the distribution board, meter-side connections (these belong to the electricity distribution company), three-phase work, anything near overhead lines, or any job you cannot isolate. Saying 'I will bring my senior' is professional, not weak.

This is general education, not a licence or a substitute for formal training.

a.text: A customer says: 'The MCB for the kitchen keeps tripping. Just put a 32 A one, I'll pay extra.' The kitchen circuit has 2.5 sq mm wire.

choices.label: Fit the 32 A MCB — customer is king
choices.feedback: This removes protection: 2.5 sq mm wire can overheat long before 32 A trips.

choices.label: Explain the risk and offer to find the cause of tripping
choices.feedback: Right — the breaker protects the wire. Find out why it trips.

b.text: You isolate the circuit and check. The customer runs a 2 kW induction, a microwave and an electric kettle together on one extension board.

choices.label: Suggest a separate 16 A circuit with proper wire for heavy appliances
choices.feedback: Excellent — the real fix is redistributing the load with proper wiring.

choices.label: Tell them to keep using the extension board but more carefully
choices.feedback: Heavy loads on extension boards are a fire risk; this does not fix the cause.

bad1.text: Months later the wire insulation inside the wall cooks and smokes. Oversizing the breaker hid the overload. The breaker must match the wire.

bad2.text: The extension board melts one evening. Luckily no one is hurt. Fix overload by redistributing load on properly sized circuits.

good.text: You give a written estimate for a new dedicated circuit, the customer agrees, and the tripping stops. You kept them safe and earned their trust.

quiz.q: What should you do FIRST on a service call about a hot regulator?
options: Ask questions, then isolate and test dead before opening
quiz.why: On a service call, ask questions first, then isolate and test dead before opening. Following safe isolation protects you.

quiz.q: In an Edison screw bulb holder, phase should connect to…
quiz.why: Phase to the centre contact reduces the chance of touching live metal when changing bulbs.

quiz.q: Who usually issues electrician permits and contractor licences in India?
quiz.why: Electrician permits and contractor licences are usually issued by the state electrical licensing authority. The rules vary by state.

quiz.q: A customer asks you to bypass the RCCB. You should…
options: Refuse politely and explain it protects lives
quiz.why: Refuse politely and explain that the RCCB protects lives. Professionals do not do unsafe work, even if paid.

quiz.q: Which job is NOT for a learner/helper?
quiz.why: Meter-side connections belong to the distribution company and trained staff. A learner or helper must not do them.

sources: ITI Electrician trade — general awareness

questions.why: Indian single-phase supply is about 230 V at 50 Hz AC.
One unit of electricity is one kilowatt-hour (kWh).

questions.q: Which device protects people from leakage current?
questions.why: An RCCB detects leakage current, the imbalance between phase and neutral, and trips to protect people.

questions.q: In the harmonised colour code, the earth wire is…
questions.why: In the harmonised colour code, green-and-yellow is earth.

questions.q: A 1150 W heater on 230 V draws about…
Why must the tester be proved after testing dead too?
options: To confirm it didn't fail during the test
questions.why: Prove the tester again after the test to confirm it didn't fail during the test. A failed tester would also read zero volts.

questions.q: An MCB trips instantly with a bang when a fan is switched on. Most likely…
questions.why: An MCB that trips instantly with a bang means very high current, which is a short circuit. An overload trips slowly.

questions.q: Why is black wire ambiguous in India?
options: It is neutral in the old scheme but can be a phase in harmonised three-phase
questions.why: Black is neutral in the old Indian scheme but can be a phase in the harmonised three-phase scheme. Mixing schemes makes colour unreliable.

questions.q: Which statement about neutral is correct?
options: Neutral is always safe to touch
Neutral is the same as earth
Neutral can carry current and become dangerous in a fault
questions.why: Neutral can carry current and can become dangerous in a fault. Treat it as potentially live. It is not the same as earth.

questions.q: The breaker rating should be chosen mainly to protect…
questions.why: A breaker should be chosen mainly to protect the wire from overheating. Its rating must match the cable.

questions.q: An RCCB trips but no MCB does when the washing machine heats water. Best interpretation?
options: Leakage to earth in the machine
questions.why: When only the RCCB trips and not an MCB, there is leakage to earth rather than overload. The fault is likely in the heating element or its wiring.

questions.q: Correct response to a person stuck to a live cable when you can't reach the switch?
options: Use a dry wooden stick to push the cable away while standing on a dry surface
questions.why: Separate the person from the cable using a dry non-conductor, like a dry wooden stick, while standing on a dry surface. Then call 112 and give CPR if needed. Water or bare hands are deadly.

questions.q: A 4 kW load runs 3 hours a day for 30 days. Units used?
questions.why: Energy = power × time × days = 4 kW × 3 h × 30 = 360 kWh, or 360 units.

questions.q: Why can't a 16 A MCB substitute for an RCCB for shock protection?
options: Dangerous shock currents (tens of mA) are far below its trip current
questions.why: A 16 A MCB only trips at currents far above the tens of mA that are dangerous to people. An RCCB (around 30 mA) is needed for shock protection.

questions.q: A homeowner joined earth to neutral to stop RCCB tripping. Why is this dangerous?
options: It hides leakage, can make metal parts live and defeats the RCCB
questions.why: Joining earth to neutral hides the leakage and defeats the RCCB. It can also make earthed metal parts live in faults, which is a serious shock risk.

courses.title: Plumbing basics for homes
courses.summary: How water comes in and goes out of an Indian home, which pipes are used where, how to fix a dripping tap and a blocked drain, and how to work as a trusted plumber.
outcomes: Learners can trace supply and drainage in a typical Indian house or flat
Learners can choose the right pipe material (CPVC, uPVC, PVC/SWR, GI, PPR) for a job
Learners can fix a dripping tap and seal threads correctly with PTFE tape
Learners can clear a blocked drain safely and explain why traps matter
Learners can estimate and quote a small plumbing job

lessons.title: How water moves through a home

scenes.text: Lakshmi runs a small paying-guest house in Hyderabad. Every summer the top-floor taps have poor flow.
Plumber Ramesh climbs to the terrace: a municipal line fills an underground sump, a pump lifts water to the overhead tank, and gravity brings it down.
'Your overhead tank is only a little higher than your top-floor shower,' he explains. 'Height gives pressure. Here there is almost none.'
He suggests a small booster pump for the top floor only. Lakshmi finally understands her own building.

steps.title: Two systems: supply and drainage
steps.body:
Every building has **two separate systems** that must never mix:

- **Supply (clean water)**: municipal line or borewell → often an **underground sump** → **pump** → **overhead tank** → down-take pipes → taps, geyser, flush tank. It is under pressure (from height or a pump).
- **Drainage (waste)**: from fixtures → traps → waste/soil pipes → inspection chambers → sewer or septic tank. It works by **gravity**, so pipes need a steady downward slope.

Grey water (basins, showers, washing) and black water (toilets) may run in separate stacks in larger buildings.

steps.title: Pressure from height
steps.body:
Each **10 metres** of water height gives about **1 bar** (≈ 1 kg/cm²) of pressure. A tank only 2 m above a shower gives roughly 0.2 bar — a weak trickle. Many modern mixers and instant geysers need more pressure than that, which is why top floors often add a **pressure pump**.

Worked example: tank base at 12 m, ground-floor tap at 1 m → height difference 11 m → about 1.1 bar at the tap (minus losses in the pipes).

steps.title: Pipe materials and where they go
steps.body:
- **CPVC**: hot and cold water supply inside homes; very common today; solvent-cement joints.
- **uPVC**: cold water supply only (not for hot water).
- **PPR**: hot and cold supply; joined by heat fusion with a special machine.
- **GI (galvanised iron)**: older buildings; threaded joints; rusts inside over years, reducing flow and colouring water.
- **PVC / SWR pipes**: drainage — soil, waste and rainwater; larger diameters (e.g. 75 mm, 110 mm).
- **HDPE**: underground/outdoor supply lines and borewells.

Common mistake: using uPVC on the geyser outlet — it softens and fails with hot water.

steps.title: Hygiene and safety basics
steps.body:
- Never allow a drainage pipe to connect into a supply pipe or tank — contamination spreads disease.
- Overhead tanks need a tight lid, an overflow pipe with a mesh, and regular cleaning (commonly every 6 months).
- Turn off the electric **pump and geyser** before working on their pipes; geyser water can scald.
- Wear gloves when dealing with drains; wash hands after.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Trace your own home: find the main valve, the tank (or pump), the geyser inlet and outlet, and where the kitchen and bathroom drains leave the building. Draw a simple map with arrows.

activity.prompt: Supply or drainage? Sort each item.

quiz.q: About how much pressure does 10 m of water height give?
quiz.why: Water pressure is about 1 bar per 10 m of height. So 10 m of water gives roughly 1 bar.

quiz.q: Which pipe is NOT suitable for hot water?
quiz.why: uPVC is only for cold water, because it softens with heat. CPVC, PPR and copper are used for hot water.
Drainage works by gravity, so pipes need a consistent downward slope. There is no pump pressure in a normal drain.

quiz.q: Why should a tank have a mesh on its overflow?
options: To keep insects and animals out
quiz.why: A mesh on the overflow keeps insects, mosquitoes and small animals out of the tank.

options: Rust and reduced flow over time
quiz.why: Old GI (galvanised iron) pipes corrode inside, causing rust and reduced flow over time.

story.title: The drip that wasted thousands of litres

scenes.text: In Chennai, Mr. Iyer's kitchen tap dripped day and night. 'Only a drop,' he said.
His granddaughter Nila measured: a cup (about 200 ml) every 10 minutes. That is over 28 litres a day.
Plumber Selvi shut the isolation valve, opened the tap and replaced a worn rubber washer in 15 minutes.
Nila calculated the water saved in a year — over 10,000 litres. Mr. Iyer started checking all taps every month.

steps.title: Why taps drip
steps.body:
- **Washer-type (compression) taps**: a rubber washer presses on a seat. When the washer wears or hardens, water seeps past → drip from the spout.
- **Quarter-turn / ceramic disc taps**: two ceramic discs. Grit or a cracked disc cartridge causes drips; you replace the cartridge.
- **Leak from the spindle/handle** (not the spout) → worn gland packing or O-ring.

Always identify which type you have before buying parts — take the old part to the shop.

steps.title: Worked example: replacing a tap washer
steps.body:
1. Close the **angle valve / isolation valve** (or main valve). Open the tap fully to drain.
2. Put a cloth in the basin so small parts don't fall down the drain.
3. Remove the handle cap and screw; unscrew the headgear with a spanner (protect chrome with a cloth).
4. Remove the old washer; fit a new one of the same size.
5. Check the seat for damage; reassemble; open valve slowly; check for drips.

Common mistakes: forgetting to close the valve, over-tightening (crushes the new washer), scratching chrome with a bare wrench.

steps.title: PTFE (thread seal) tape — the right way
steps.body:
Thread tape seals the tiny gaps in threaded joints.

- Wrap it **in the same direction the fitting tightens** — clockwise when you look at the end of the male thread. Wrapped backwards, it unwinds as you screw in.
- Typically **3–5 wraps**, keeping it flat and starting one thread back from the end so tape doesn't enter the pipe.
- Do not use tape on joints that seal with a rubber washer or O-ring (like flexible connectors) — the washer does the sealing.
- Hand-tight plus a little more with a spanner; plastic fittings crack if forced.

steps.title: Finding hidden leaks
steps.body:
- **Meter test**: close all taps, note the water meter reading, wait an hour; if it moves, there is a leak.
- **Toilet cistern test**: a few drops of food colour in the cistern; if colour appears in the pan without flushing, the flapper/valve leaks.
- **Damp patches, peeling paint, fungus** on walls often trace back to concealed pipe joints or bathroom floor waterproofing failures.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check every tap at home for drips and every cistern with the colour test. List what you find and what part each would need (washer, cartridge, flapper).

statements.s: PTFE tape should be wrapped clockwise when looking at the end of the male thread.
statements.why: That matches the tightening direction so the tape does not unravel.

statements.s: You should always add PTFE tape to connectors that seal with a rubber washer.
statements.why: Washers/O-rings seal those joints; tape can stop them seating.

statements.s: A drip from the spout of a washer tap usually means a worn washer.
statements.why: The washer no longer seals against the seat.

statements.s: Closing the isolation valve is optional when replacing a washer.
statements.why: Without closing it, water will gush out when you open the tap head.

statements.s: A moving water meter with all taps closed suggests a leak.
statements.why: No use should mean no flow.

quiz.q: A ceramic-disc tap drips. What do you usually replace?
quiz.why: A ceramic-disc tap uses a cartridge. When it drips, you usually replace the cartridge. The rubber washer is for older tap types.

quiz.q: Water leaks from around the handle spindle. Likely cause?
quiz.why: A leak around the handle spindle usually comes from worn gland packing or an O-ring. A worn washer causes a drip from the spout.

quiz.q: How many wraps of PTFE tape are typical?
quiz.why: About 3–5 neat wraps of PTFE tape is typical for household threads. Too little leaks and too much makes it hard to fit.

quiz.q: A cup of 200 ml every 10 minutes is about how much per day?
quiz.why: 10 minutes per cup gives 6 cups per hour, so 144 cups a day. 144 × 0.2 L = 28.8 L.

quiz.q: Best first step before opening a tap head?
quiz.why: Close the isolation valve first, so the water supply is cut before you open the tap head.

scenes.text: A guest at Anita's homestay in Shimla complained of a sewer smell in an unused bathroom.
Plumber Thakur ji poured a bucket of water into the floor trap. The smell disappeared within an hour.
'The trap's water seal dried up,' he said. 'That little pool of water is what stops sewer gas coming in.'
Anita added 'pour water into unused traps weekly' to her housekeeping checklist.

steps.title: What a trap does
steps.body:
A **trap** (P-trap, S-trap, bottle trap, floor trap/Nahani trap) is a bend that always holds a little water — the **water seal**. This seal blocks foul gases and insects from coming up the drain.

Seals are lost by: drying out (unused fixtures), siphoning (poor venting), or cracks. Fix: refill with water; for repeated loss, check venting and the trap itself.

steps.title: Clearing a blocked drain — safely, in order
steps.body:
1. **Remove what you can see**: hair from the floor trap grating, food from the sink strainer.
2. **Plunger**: cover the overflow hole with a wet cloth, ensure some water in the basin, plunge firmly 10–15 times.
3. **Open the bottle trap** under the basin (bucket underneath) and clean it.
4. **Drain auger / snake** for deeper blockages.
5. Hot (not boiling, for PVC) water helps with grease in kitchen sinks.

Never **mix chemical drain cleaners** with each other or with bleach/acid — toxic gas and burns can result. If you use one, follow the label, wear gloves and eye protection, and never plunge after adding chemicals (splash risk).

steps.title: Slope matters
steps.body: Horizontal drainage pipes need a steady fall. A common rule of thumb for small-diameter waste pipes is about **1 in 40 to 1 in 60** (e.g. 2.5 cm drop for each 1–1.5 m). Too flat → solids settle and block; dips (bellies) collect sludge. Use a spirit level while fixing clamps.

steps.title: Things that block drains
steps.body: Cooking oil and ghee (solidifies), tea leaves, rice, hair, wet wipes, sanitary pads, cotton buds, plastic, construction debris. Toilets should receive only human waste and toilet paper. Educating customers prevents repeat calls.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find every trap in your home (kitchen sink, wash basin, floor traps, washing machine outlet). Clean one strainer and note what you find. Pour water into any trap that hasn't been used for a week.

activity.prompt: Order the drain-clearing steps from least to most invasive.
items: Remove visible hair or food from the strainer
Use a plunger with the overflow covered
Open and clean the bottle trap over a bucket
Use a drain auger for deeper blockages
Call for main-line clearing if still blocked

quiz.q: What stops sewer gas entering through a floor trap?
quiz.why: The trap's standing water, the water seal, stops sewer gas from entering through a floor trap.

quiz.q: An unused bathroom smells of sewage. First check?
quiz.why: If an unused bathroom smells of sewage, refill the trap with water first. The seal dries up if it is not used, and then sewer gas comes through.

quiz.q: Why cover the basin overflow while plunging?
options: So the pressure goes into the blockage, not out the overflow
quiz.why: Cover the overflow while plunging so the pressure goes into the blockage and not out of the overflow.

quiz.q: Mixing drain chemicals with bleach can…
quiz.why: Mixing drain chemicals with bleach can release toxic gas. Never mix cleaning chemicals.

quiz.q: A horizontal drain laid completely flat will…
quiz.why: A horizontal drain laid flat has no slope to carry solids, so they settle and cause blockages. Drains need a consistent slope.

lessons.title: Working as a plumber: estimates and customers

scenes.text: In Bhopal, Farhan and Joseph both quote for a bathroom pipe replacement.
Farhan says 'around four–five thousand, see as we go'. Joseph writes a list: materials, labour, time, and what is not included (tiles).
The customer chooses Joseph even though he is slightly more expensive. 'I know exactly what I'm paying for.'
Joseph finishes on time, cleans up and leaves a photo record of the concealed pipes. He gets three referrals.

steps.title: How to build a simple estimate
steps.body:
Break the job into lines:

- **Materials**: pipe length + 10% wastage, fittings (elbows, tees, unions, valves), solvent cement, tape, clamps.
- **Labour**: hours × rate (or a fixed rate per point/fitting, as is common locally).
- **Extras**: chiselling and patching walls, tile removal, debris disposal, transport.
- **Exclusions**: say clearly what is not included.
- **Validity**: e.g. 'valid for 15 days' as prices change.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Replacing 12 m of CPVC with 10 fittings:

- Pipe: 12 m + 10% = 13.2 m → buy enough standard lengths to cover it
- Fittings and cement: listed with shop prices
- Labour: 1 plumber + 1 helper, 1 day
- Wall chasing and patching: separate line

Total = materials + labour + extras. Add a small contingency (5–10%) for surprises and **tell the customer** it is there.

steps.title: Customer trust
steps.body:
- Show the old damaged part; explain the cause.
- Take **photos of concealed pipes** before tiling — future repairs become easy.
- Pressure-test new lines before closing walls.
- Give a simple warranty on your workmanship and honour it.
- Accept UPI/receipts and keep records.

steps.title: Training routes
steps.body: Plumber trades are offered at ITIs and as short-term skill courses through national skilling schemes and sector skill councils. Growth paths: site plumber → supervisor → contractor; specialisations in solar water heating, fire-fighting lines, rainwater harvesting and building services (MEP).

a.text: While replacing a tap, you notice the wall behind is damp and the concealed joint is leaking. The customer only asked for a tap.

choices.label: Fix the tap and leave quietly
choices.feedback: The hidden leak will damage the wall and they'll blame the last plumber — you.

choices.label: Show them the damp area, explain, and offer a separate quote

b.text: The customer says, 'Just do it today, how much?' You haven't opened the wall yet.

choices.label: Give a firm low price to win the job
choices.feedback: Unknown hidden damage could make you lose money or cut corners.

choices.label: Give a range, explain what could change it, and agree before extra work
choices.feedback: Clear, fair and safe for both sides.

e1.text: Two months later the tiles fall. The customer posts a bad review. Always report what you see.

e2.text: The joint is badly corroded and you need extra fittings and a whole day. You either lose money or argue. Ranges with conditions avoid this.

e3.text: You find two corroded joints, explain, replace them within the agreed range, pressure-test and photograph. A loyal customer is born.

quiz.q: Why add about 10% to pipe length in an estimate?
quiz.why: Add about 10% to pipe length for wastage and cuts. Fitting and cutting always waste some pipe.

quiz.q: Why photograph concealed pipes before tiling?
options: To locate pipes easily in future repairs
quiz.why: Photograph concealed pipes before tiling so you can find them in future repairs. That avoids drilling into pipes and saves time.

quiz.q: When should new concealed lines be pressure-tested?
quiz.why: Pressure-test new concealed lines before closing the walls. Any leaks can then be fixed easily.
A good estimate has line items, exclusions and a validity period. Clear items build trust.

questions.q: Which pipe is common for hot and cold supply in Indian homes today?
questions.why: CPVC is commonly used for both hot and cold water supply in Indian homes. uPVC is for cold water only.

options: Hold a water seal against sewer gas
questions.why: A trap holds a water seal that blocks sewer gas and insects from coming up the drain.

questions.q: To fix a spout drip on a washer tap you usually replace…
questions.why: A drip from the spout of a washer tap is usually a worn washer, so you replace the washer.
Wrap PTFE tape in the tightening direction, so the tape tightens with the joint instead of unwinding.

questions.q: A tank 5 m above a tap gives roughly…
questions.why: Pressure is about 1 bar per 10 m of height, so 5 m gives roughly 0.5 bar.

questions.q: Which should never go down a toilet?
questions.why: Wet wipes and pads should never go down a toilet, because they don't break down and cause blockages. Toilet paper does break down.

questions.q: Why is uPVC wrong for a geyser outlet?
options: It is rated for cold water and softens with heat
questions.why: uPVC is rated for cold water and softens with heat, so it is wrong for a geyser outlet. Use CPVC, PPR or copper.

questions.q: With all taps closed, the water meter moves. This shows…
questions.why: If the meter moves with all taps closed, water is going somewhere, so there is likely a leak. Investigate.

questions.q: Covering the overflow while plunging helps because…
options: Pressure is directed at the blockage
questions.why: Covering the overflow directs the pressure from the plunger at the blockage, rather than letting it escape through the overflow.

questions.q: Repeated loss of trap seal even when fixtures are used may indicate…
questions.why: Repeated loss of the trap seal, even with normal use, may be due to siphoning from poor venting. Proper vent pipes prevent it.

questions.q: Tap leaks from the handle, not the spout. Which part?
questions.why: A leak from the handle comes from the gland packing or O-ring around the spindle. A spout drip is the washer or cartridge.

questions.q: Best way to handle unknown hidden damage in a quote?
options: Give a range, state conditions, agree before extra work
questions.why: For unknown hidden damage, give a range, state the conditions, and agree before doing extra work. This is fair to both sides.

questions.q: A horizontal waste pipe has a dip (belly) in the middle. What happens over time?
questions.why: A dip (belly) in a horizontal waste pipe holds water and solids, so sludge collects and blockages recur.

questions.q: Which cross-connection is most dangerous to health?
options: Drainage connected into a supply tank or pipe
questions.why: Connecting drainage into a supply tank or pipe can contaminate drinking water with sewage and spread disease. That is the most dangerous cross-connection.

courses.title: Carpentry and woodwork basics
courses.summary: Know your woods and boards, measure and mark accurately, use hand and power tools safely, and make strong joints with a good finish.
outcomes: Learners can choose between solid wood, plywood (MR/BWR/BWP), MDF and particle board
Learners can measure, mark and plan cuts with minimum waste
Learners can use common hand and power tools with the right safety habits
Learners can choose and make basic joints and finish wood properly

scenes.text: Rekha in Mumbai got new kitchen cabinets. Within one monsoon the sink cabinet's base swelled and crumbled.
Carpenter Imran inspected it: 'This is ordinary particle board under the sink. Water and this board are enemies.'
He rebuilt it with waterproof-grade plywood and sealed edges with edge-banding.
Two monsoons later it was perfect. Rekha learned: the board matters as much as the design.

steps.title: Solid wood
steps.body:
Commonly used Indian timbers include **teak (sagwan)** — durable, stable, naturally resists termites and moisture, expensive; **sal** — very strong, used for door frames and structural work; **sheesham (Indian rosewood)** — hard, attractive grain, used for furniture; **mango wood** and **rubberwood** — affordable furniture woods that need proper seasoning/treatment.

Wood moves with humidity: it expands and shrinks across the grain much more than along it. Well-**seasoned** (dried) wood moves less and cracks less.

steps.title: Engineered boards
steps.body:
- **Plywood**: thin veneers glued in alternating grain directions — strong and stable. Grades you will hear: **MR** (moisture resistant, for dry interiors like wardrobes), **BWR** (boiling-water resistant) and **BWP / marine** (boiling-water proof, for kitchens, bathrooms, damp areas). Check for the relevant IS marking on the sheet.
- **Blockboard**: wooden strips core with veneer faces — good for long shelves and doors that shouldn't sag.
- **MDF**: smooth, paints well, good for shutters and CNC designs; swells badly if wet; holds screws poorly at edges.
- **Particle board**: cheapest; for low-cost dry-area furniture only.

Standard sheet size in India: **8 ft × 4 ft** (about 2440 × 1220 mm). Common thicknesses: 6, 9, 12, 18/19 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Particle board or MR ply under a sink or in a bathroom.
- Leaving board edges unsealed (water enters through edges first).
- Using unseasoned wood — doors warp and joints open.
- Ignoring termites: treat wood, keep it off damp walls, inspect regularly.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing materials for a kitchen
steps.body:
- Carcass under sink: **BWP / marine ply**, edges banded, with a water-resistant laminate.
- Wall cabinets: BWR ply is commonly used.
- Shutters: BWP ply or good-quality boards with laminate/acrylic.
- Shelves over 90 cm long: 18/19 mm ply or blockboard, or add a middle support to prevent sag.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Look at furniture at home or in a shop. Look at an exposed edge: can you see layers (plywood), strips (blockboard), uniform fibre (MDF), or chips (particle board)? Make a list.

activity.prompt: Match the material with its best use.
pairs: Painted CNC-cut panel in a dry room

quiz.q: Which plywood grade suits a bathroom vanity?
quiz.why: For a bathroom vanity, use BWP (boiling-water-proof) or marine ply, which is made for damp areas. MR ply, MDF and particle board swell with moisture.

quiz.q: Standard Indian board sheet size is…
quiz.why: The standard Indian board sheet is 8 × 4 ft, about 2440 × 1220 mm.
Wood moves much more across the grain than along it, as moisture changes. So allow for movement across the grain.

quiz.q: Why seal or edge-band board edges?
quiz.why: Board edges absorb moisture fastest, so sealing or edge-banding them stops water getting in and swelling the board.

quiz.q: Which board swells badly when wet and holds edge screws poorly?
quiz.why: MDF swells badly when wet and holds screws poorly at the edges. BWP ply and solid woods like sal or teak cope better.

story.title: The 2 mm that ruined a drawer

scenes.text: Apprentice Karan in Ludhiana cut eight drawer sides, each measured from the previous piece.
The small errors added up; the last drawer was 6 mm short and wobbled.
Master carpenter Gurdeep ji showed him: mark all pieces from one reference edge, use a stop block, and cut on the waste side of the line.
The next set fit perfectly. 'Accuracy is a habit, not luck,' said Gurdeep ji.

steps.title: Measuring and marking tools
steps.body:
- **Measuring tape** (metric and imperial) and **steel rule**.
- **Try square** — checks and marks 90°.
- **Combination square / sliding bevel** — 45° and other angles.
- **Marking gauge** — scratches a line parallel to an edge.
- **Sharp pencil or marking knife** — a thick pencil line can be 1 mm wide!

Units: 1 inch = **25.4 mm**; 1 foot = 12 inches = **304.8 mm**. Pick one system per project to avoid conversion errors.

steps.title: Good marking habits
steps.body:
- Choose a straight **reference edge** and square end; measure everything from it.
- Mark with a 'V' or tick to show the exact point, not a blob.
- Mark the **waste side** with an X and cut on that side of the line — the saw blade itself removes 2–3 mm (the **kerf**).
- For identical parts, use a **stop block** or cut them together.
- Check diagonals of a frame: if both diagonals are equal, it is square.

steps.title: Worked example: cutting list from an 8 × 4 sheet
steps.body:
You need shelves 600 mm × 300 mm from a 2440 × 1220 mm sheet, with a 3 mm kerf.

- Across the 1220 mm width: 300 + 3 + 300 + 3 + 300 + 3 + 300 = 1209 mm → **4 strips** fit (11 mm left).
- Along 2440 mm: 600 + 3 + 600 + 3 + 600 + 3 + 600 = 2409 mm → **4 pieces** per strip.
- Total = 4 × 4 = **16 shelves** from one sheet.

Forgetting kerf is the most common planning mistake — 600 × 4 = 2400 looks like it fits, but each cut eats wood.

steps.title: Check diagonals: the carpenter's square test
steps.body: For a rectangle 900 mm × 1200 mm, the diagonal should be √(900² + 1200²) = **1500 mm** (a 3-4-5 triangle scaled up). Measure both diagonals; adjust until they match. This works for doors, frames and even room layouts.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Plan a cutting list on paper for a small bookshelf: 2 sides 900 × 250 mm, 4 shelves 600 × 250 mm, top 640 × 250 mm. How many can you fit in a half sheet (1220 × 1220 mm) allowing 3 mm kerf?

activity.prompt: A rectangular frame is 600 mm × 800 mm. What should each diagonal measure if it is perfectly square?

options: The width of material the blade removes
quiz.why: Kerf is the width of material the saw blade removes. Plan for it in every cut, or your parts will come out short.

quiz.q: Why measure all parts from one reference edge?
quiz.why: Measure all parts from one reference edge so small errors don't add up along the way.

quiz.q: A frame's diagonals are 1502 mm and 1490 mm. The frame is…
quiz.why: A square or rectangular frame has equal diagonals. 1502 mm and 1490 mm are unequal, so the frame is out of square.

quiz.q: Which side of the line should you cut on?
quiz.why: Cut on the waste side of the line, so the part you keep stays at its marked size. Cutting on the line removes some of the part.

scenes.text: In a furniture unit in Jodhpur, helper Vikram fed a narrow strip into the table saw with his fingers.
Supervisor Asha stopped the machine: 'Fingers never go within a hand's width of the blade. Use the push stick.'
She made everyone wear goggles and ear protection and keep the riving knife and guard in place.
That year the unit had zero injuries. Vikram now trains new helpers.

steps.title: Hand tools every carpenter uses
steps.body:
- **Saws**: rip saw (along the grain), crosscut saw (across the grain), tenon/back saw for joints, coping saw for curves.
- **Chisels** for joints and cleaning corners; keep them sharp — a blunt chisel slips.
- **Planes** to flatten and smooth.
- **Hammer, mallet, screwdrivers, clamps**, and a **drill** with wood bits.

Keep tools sharp, clean and stored; a sharp tool needs less force and is safer.

steps.title: Power tools
steps.body:
- **Circular saw / table saw** for straight cuts; **jigsaw** for curves; **router** for edges and grooves; **drill-driver**; **orbital sander**.

Before use: check the cable and plug, blade condition and guard; clamp the work; unplug before changing blades or bits.

steps.title: Safety rules that save fingers and eyes
steps.body:
- **Eye protection** always; **ear protection** for saws and routers; **dust mask** for sanding, MDF dust especially.
- No loose sleeves, gloves near spinning blades (they can be pulled in), or dangling jewellery; tie long hair.
- Use **push sticks** for narrow cuts; never reach over a running blade.
- Keep guards and riving knives fitted.
- Wait for the blade to stop fully.
- Keep the floor clear of offcuts and cables.

steps.title: Screws, nails and pilot holes
steps.body:
- Drill a **pilot hole** before screwing into hardwood or near edges to prevent splitting.
- Countersink so screw heads sit flush.
- Nails hold well against sideways loads but can pull out; screws resist pull-out; glue + screws is strongest for furniture.
- In board edges, use screws designed for boards and keep away from the very edge.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a personal safety card for any power tool you'll use: goggles, ear protection, mask, cable check, guard on, clamp work, push stick, unplug to change blade.

activity.prompt: Before switching on a table saw, I have…
items: Put on safety goggles and ear protection
Removed loose sleeves and jewellery, tied long hair
Checked the blade is sharp and the guard and riving knife are fitted
Set the fence and blade height correctly
Got a push stick within reach
Cleared offcuts and cables from the floor
Made sure no one is standing in line behind the blade

quiz.q: Which saw is meant for cutting along the grain?
quiz.why: A rip saw is made for cutting along the grain. A crosscut saw cuts across the grain.

quiz.q: Why is a blunt chisel more dangerous?
options: It needs more force and slips
quiz.why: A blunt chisel needs more force, so it is likelier to slip and cause injury. Sharp tools are safer.

quiz.q: Why avoid gloves near a spinning blade?
options: They can be caught and pull your hand in
quiz.why: Avoid gloves near a spinning blade, because they can be caught and pull your hand in.

quiz.q: Before changing a router bit you should…
quiz.why: Unplug the router before changing a bit, so it can't start accidentally.

quiz.q: Why drill a pilot hole in hardwood?
quiz.why: Drill a pilot hole in hardwood so the screw doesn't split the wood.

scenes.text: Sneha in Mysuru found her grandfather's 60-year-old chair still solid. Her new flat-pack chair wobbled within a year.
Carpenter Manjunath showed her the old chair's mortise-and-tenon joints and the new one's simple butt joints with small screws.
He re-glued and dowelled the new chair, sanded it from 120 to 220 grit, and finished it with PU polish.
Sneha learned that joints and finish decide whether furniture lasts years or decades.

steps.title: Common joints
steps.body:
- **Butt joint**: two pieces meet end-to-face; weakest; needs screws, dowels or brackets.
- **Lap / halving joint**: each piece cut half-depth — frames.
- **Dado / housing**: groove holds a shelf — strong for bookshelves.
- **Rebate (rabbet)**: step along an edge — cabinet backs.
- **Dowel joint**: wooden pins + glue — simple and strong when aligned.
- **Mortise and tenon**: tongue fits a slot — chairs, tables, doors; very strong.
- **Dovetail**: interlocking — drawer corners; resists pulling apart.

steps.title: Gluing well
steps.body:
- Use the right adhesive: PVA/synthetic resin wood glue for interiors; waterproof adhesives for wet areas.
- Surfaces must be clean, flat and fit well — glue doesn't fill big gaps.
- **Clamp** with even pressure, check square, wipe squeeze-out with a damp cloth before it dries.
- Respect the drying/curing time on the label before loading the joint.

steps.title: Sanding and finishing
steps.body:
- Sand **with the grain**, going through grits: e.g. **80 → 120 → 180 → 220**. Don't skip more than one step; each grit removes the scratches of the previous.
- Remove dust before finishing.
- Finishes: **wood stain** (colour), **melamine** and **PU (polyurethane)** polishes (durable, common in India), **French polish** (traditional shellac, beautiful but less water-resistant), **laminates and veneers** for boards, paint for MDF.
- Apply thin coats; sand lightly with fine grit between coats.

steps.title: Finishing safety
steps.body: Solvents and polishes are flammable and their fumes harmful: ventilate, avoid sparks and smoking, wear a suitable mask and gloves. **Oily rags can self-heat and catch fire** — spread them flat outdoors to dry or soak in water before disposal.

steps.title: Earning from carpentry
steps.body: Paths include: modular kitchen and wardrobe installation, furniture repair and polishing, site carpentry (doors, frames, formwork), CNC operation, and your own workshop. Keep a portfolio of before/after photos, give written estimates, and learn design basics and customer communication — they lift income as much as skill does.

cards.back: A tongue (tenon) fits a slot (mortise). Very strong — chairs, tables, doors.
Interlocking wedge-shaped pins and tails; resists pulling apart — drawers.

A step cut along an edge, e.g. for a cabinet back.
End against face; weakest; needs screws, dowels or brackets.
Coarse to fine, with the grain: 80 → 120 → 180 → 220.
Can self-heat and ignite — dry flat outdoors or soak in water.

quiz.q: Strongest traditional joint for a chair leg-to-rail?
quiz.why: A mortise and tenon is the strongest traditional joint for a chair leg to rail, and lasts long. A butt joint or nailing is weak.

quiz.q: Which joint is classic for drawer corners?
quiz.why: Dovetails are the classic drawer-corner joint, because the interlocking shape resists being pulled apart.
Sand from coarse to fine: 80 → 120 → 180 → 220. Each grit removes the scratches left by the previous one.
Rags with oily finishes can catch fire on their own, because the oils oxidise and give off heat. Lay them out flat to dry or put them in water.

options: Surfaces fit well and are clamped
quiz.why: Glue joints work best when the surfaces fit well and are clamped. Glue is not a gap filler.

questions.q: Which board suits wet areas best?
questions.why: BWP (boiling-water-proof) or marine ply suits wet areas. MR ply, MDF and particle board don't cope with a lot of water.
A try square checks and marks 90° angles.

questions.q: Which protection is needed when sanding MDF?
questions.why: MDF dust is fine and harmful to breathe, so wear a dust mask when sanding it.

options: Keep fingers away from the blade on narrow cuts
questions.why: A push stick keeps your fingers away from the blade when making narrow cuts on a table saw.

questions.q: Which joint uses a groove to hold a shelf?
questions.why: A dado (or housing) joint is a groove cut across a board to hold a shelf. A rebate is a step along an edge.
Teak is prized because it is durable and stable, and its natural oils resist moisture and termites.

questions.q: A 900 × 1200 mm frame should have diagonals of…
questions.why: For a 900 × 1200 mm frame, the diagonal is √(900² + 1200²) = √2,250,000 = 1500 mm. Equal diagonals show it is square.

questions.q: Forgetting kerf in a cutting plan results in…
options: Parts slightly short or one fewer piece
questions.why: Each cut removes the blade's width (kerf). Forgetting it makes parts slightly short, or leaves you one piece fewer.

questions.q: Which finish is traditional, beautiful but less water-resistant?
questions.why: French polish is a traditional, beautiful shellac finish, but water marks it. It is less water-resistant than PU or epoxy.

questions.q: A 1.2 m shelf in 12 mm MDF is sagging. Best fix?
options: Use 18/19 mm ply or blockboard, or add a middle support
questions.why: A 12 mm MDF shelf over 1.2 m will sag. Use a thicker, stiffer board like 18/19 mm ply or blockboard, or add a middle support.
Without clamping, the surfaces don't press together, so the glue joint is weaker and may have gaps. Pressure ensures close contact.

questions.q: Why does wood movement matter in a solid-wood tabletop?
options: Wood only moves along its length
The top expands/shrinks across the grain; fix it so it can move or it may crack
questions.why: Solid wood expands and shrinks across the grain with the seasons. A tabletop must be fixed so it can move, or it may crack.

questions.q: You need 20 shelves of 600 × 300 mm with 3 mm kerf. How many 8 × 4 sheets?
questions.why: One 8 × 4 sheet (2440 × 1220 mm) can give about 16 shelves of 600 × 300 mm even with kerf. So 20 shelves need 2 sheets.

story.title: It lights up but shows nothing

scenes.text: Asha's laptop fan spins and the power LED lights, but the screen stays black.
The boot chain has stages; knowing which one failed saves hours.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body: 1) Power rails come up and the embedded controller (EC) starts. 2) CPU runs firmware (BIOS/UEFI). 3) **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) checks CPU, memory and basic hardware. 4) Firmware finds a boot device. 5) Bootloader starts the operating system.

steps.title: Beep codes are not universal
steps.body: Different firmware makers use different patterns, and many modern laptops have no speaker at all and use LED blink codes or on-screen messages. Always check the maker's table for that model.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: Power the laptop off, unplug the charger and, where the maker allows it, disconnect the internal battery before touching internals. Use an ESD strap or touch bare metal first. Work only on laptops you own or are authorised to service; do not open sealed or glued devices outside the maker's guidance.

scenes.text: Farhan buys DDR5 for a laptop that uses DDR4. It does not fit.
Notches and pin counts keep generations apart.

steps.title: RAM facts
steps.body: Laptop memory is SO-DIMM. DDR4 SO-DIMM has 260 pins; DDR5 SO-DIMM has 262. They are keyed differently and not interchangeable. Some ultrabooks have soldered RAM that cannot be upgraded.

steps.title: Capacity and channels

scenes.text: A customer's SSD was formatted and then used for months.

steps.title: Recovery reality
steps.body: On SSDs with TRIM, deleted data may be physically erased quickly and cannot be recovered. Mechanical failure of HDDs needs a clean-room lab; DIY opening makes things worse. Stop writing to the drive immediately.

scenes.text: Dhruv's gaming laptop sounds like a jet and drops frames after ten minutes.

steps.title: Heat path
steps.body: Heat flows from the chip to a heat spreader, through thermal paste or pads to a copper heatsink with heat pipes, then fins, where the fan blows it out. Any weak link raises temperature.

steps.title: Throttling
steps.body: Chips protect themselves: when they near their maximum junction temperature (commonly around 100 degrees C for many CPUs), they reduce clock speed. That is **thermal throttling**.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: Power the laptop off, unplug the charger and, where the maker allows it, disconnect the internal battery before opening it. Use an ESD strap, work on a non-conductive surface and keep a small container for screws. Opening some devices may void the warranty; follow the service manual for the exact model.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Record idle and loaded temperatures and fan RPM using a monitoring tool; load the CPU for ten minutes; note when clock speed drops.

steps.title: Normal ranges
steps.body: Idle 35-50 degrees C and loaded 70-90 degrees C are common; sustained readings near 95-100 degrees C show a cooling problem. Limits vary by chip.

steps.title: Never block vents
steps.body: Use hard flat surfaces. Soft beds and pillows block intakes.

steps.title: Fans spin freely
steps.body: When using compressed air, hold the fan blades still. Over-spinning can damage the motor or bearings. Do not use a vacuum cleaner on electronics because static can build up.

steps.title: Pads
steps.body: Use the right thickness thermal pads on memory/VRM; too thick lifts the heatsink off the die.

courses.title: Laptop hardware 3 · Motherboard power rails at a basic level
courses.summary: Understand how a laptop turns adapter power into the voltages a board needs, and take first-level measurements safely.
outcomes: Describe the adapter-to-rail power tree

scenes.text: A senior technician draws a tree: adapter at the root, battery charger, then always-on rails, then main rails.
Each branch must be present before the next one starts.

steps.title: Typical tree
steps.body: 1) Adapter (for example about 19 V) feeds the charger/power-path circuit. 2) The embedded controller gets always-on power (for example 3.3 V/5 V standby). 3) Pressing power asks the EC to enable main rails in order. 4) Each rail reports **power-good**. 5) When all are good, reset is released and the CPU starts.

steps.title: Battery pack voltage
steps.body: A 3-cell series pack is nominally 3 x 3.7 = 11.1 V and up to 3 x 4.2 = 12.6 V when full.

steps.title: Board-level work is for trained people
steps.body: Never short rails with probes. A slipped probe can destroy chips. Use insulated probes and a current-limited supply. Power the laptop off, unplug the charger and, where the maker allows it, disconnect the internal battery before opening it. Use an ESD strap, work on a non-conductive surface and keep a small container for screws. Opening some devices may void the warranty; follow the service manual for the exact model.

steps.title: Voltage drop
steps.body: A cable with 0.2 ohm carrying 3 A drops V = I x R = 0.6 V.

steps.title: Mind the polarity

courses.title: Phone repair 1 · Bench safety, ESD & lithium batteries
courses.summary: Set up a safe phone-repair bench: electrostatic discharge control, lithium-ion cell hazards, swollen-battery handling, chemicals, eye and fire safety.
outcomes: Set up an ESD-safe bench with correct grounding

scenes.text: Arjun, a new technician, pries a phone battery out with a steel screwdriver. The tip slices the pouch and the cell hisses and smokes.
His senior drags the phone into a metal tray and uses a sand bucket. Nobody is hurt, but the lesson is clear: the bench must be set up before the first screw.

steps.title: The three hazard families
steps.body: A phone bench has three hazards: **electrical** (battery short circuits, mains chargers), **thermal/chemical** (lithium-ion fires, heat guns, solvents) and **electrostatic** (ESD that silently kills chips). Good practice means controlling each one *before* work starts.

steps.title: Never use metal tools near a battery
steps.body: A steel tool that bridges a pouch cell or a connector can cause a short circuit, heat and fire. Use plastic spudgers and non-conductive tweezers near cells. Safety first: this course teaches repair of consumer electronics for learning. Work only on devices you own or have permission to repair, follow the maker's service guidance, and stop if you are unsure. Fires from damaged lithium cells are real - keep a metal tray or sand bucket and a CO2/ABC extinguisher in the work area.

steps.title: Bench layout
steps.body:
- Anti-static mat connected to earth through a 1 megohm resistor
- Good light and magnification
- Metal tray for removed batteries
- Fire extinguisher within reach
- Clear, uncluttered surface, no drinks or loose wires

lessons.title: Lab: ESD control on the bench

scenes.text: A repair shop sees repeat failures: phones that worked on arrival die after reassembly. The owner suspects bad parts.
An audit shows technicians on synthetic carpet, no strap, handling boards by the connectors. Static was the culprit.

steps.title: What ESD is
steps.body: You feel a static spark only above roughly 3,000 V, but many chips can be damaged by 100 V or less. So **damage happens invisibly** - the part may fail later, which is called a latent failure.

steps.title: Correct strap setup
steps.body: A wrist strap has a built-in series resistor of about **1 megohm**, so that any charge drains slowly and safely and a mains fault cannot pass through you. The strap clip goes to the mat grounding point, which connects to a proper earth.

steps.title: Habits that help
steps.body:
- Touch the mat before touching boards
- Hold boards by edges
- Keep boards in anti-static bags
- Avoid wool, synthetic carpet and dry air; humidity of 40-60% helps

scenes.text: Meena brings in a phone whose back glass has lifted and the screen is curving up. She says it still charges.
Charging it would be a gamble: a swollen cell has gas inside from electrolyte breakdown and can vent or ignite.

steps.title: Swollen means danger
steps.body: A swollen Li-ion cell must not be charged, flexed, pierced or heated. Tell the customer to stop using the phone. Handle with insulated gloves in a ventilated area.

steps.title: Safe removal principle
steps.body: Disconnect the battery connector first, then loosen the adhesive using a **small amount of isopropyl alcohol (IPA 90%+)** under the cell, working slowly. Never pry hard or bend the cell. Place it in a metal tray, tape the terminals, and pass to e-waste/battery recycling.

steps.title: Why cells swell
steps.body: Heat, overcharge, age and manufacturing faults decompose the electrolyte and produce gas. The cell cannot be "repaired"; it must be replaced.

steps.title: Press down more than you turn
steps.body: Apply firm downward pressure with a well-fitting bit and turn slowly. Most stripped screws come from the wrong bit or too little downward force.

steps.title: Heat guns and plates
steps.body: Adhesive on phone screens is softened at roughly 70-80 degrees C on a controlled heat plate, never a naked flame. Overheating burns OLED panels and swells batteries.

courses.summary: Use a digital multimeter, bench power supply and a diagnosis flowchart to turn a vague complaint into a located fault.

steps.title: The four modes you need
steps.body: **DC volts** for batteries and rails, **resistance** for tracking shorts (device power off), **continuity** (beep) for traces and fuses, and **diode mode** for checking rails against a known-good board.

steps.title: Probe discipline
steps.body: Use fine probes or sharpened tips, one hand on the probes, and never bridge two pins. Always power off and remove the battery before measuring resistance.

steps.title: Typical Li-ion voltages
steps.body: A healthy cell sits roughly between 3.0 V (empty) and 4.2 V (full) for standard cells, with about 3.7 V nominal. Some newer cells charge to 4.35-4.4 V and have nominal about 3.85 V. Do not charge a deeply discharged or swollen cell.

scenes.text: A phone is connected to a bench supply set to about 4 V with a current limit. The current meter shows 0.00 A.
Different current readings point to different fault families.

steps.title: Teaching guide (typical values vary by model)
steps.body:
- **0.00 A, no change**: open path (battery connector, power button flex, dead PMIC output) or supply not seen
- **Small current that stays steady** (tens of mA): board is partly alive but not booting
- **Very high current that clamps the supply**: short circuit on a rail
- **Current rising in steps then dropping**: normal boot attempt

steps.title: Limit the current
steps.body: Set the supply current limit modestly (for example 1 A) when probing unknown faults so a short does not burn the board.

steps.title: Compare with a known-good phone
steps.body: Model-specific boot current signatures are the best reference. Keep a notebook of healthy values.

steps.title: What fails

steps.title: LCD vs OLED
steps.body: An LCD needs a backlight; an OLED emits its own light and shows true blacks. OLED panels are more fragile to heat and pressure.

steps.title: Opening
steps.body: Heat the edges to roughly 70-80 degrees C on a controlled plate for a few minutes, apply a suction handle, make a small gap, and slide thin opening picks around the frame. Do not insert tools deep; the display flex runs near one edge.

steps.title: Cut the adhesive gradually

steps.body: Each charge cycle slightly reduces capacity. Heat speeds it up. Many manufacturers rate batteries for around 500 full cycles to about 80% of original capacity (varies by model).

steps.title: Removing
steps.body: Disconnect connector. For pull-tab adhesives, pull each tab slowly at a low angle along the surface. For tough glue, apply IPA at the edge and work a plastic card under the cell.
